design: Cross-country panel combining peering port pricing with proprietary IP-transit pricing data, 2019-2024
title: Dissecting the cost of peering: Global evidence from internet exchange points (IXPs)
data: Publicly available peering port pricing combined with proprietary IP-transit pricing data
findings: Peering costs are substantially lower than IP-transit costs across the global sample. Larger cost savings from peering relative to transit are associated with lower broadband prices for consumers, expanded mobile network coverage, and higher overall telecommunications revenues. These associations are most pronounced in moderately regulated economies and in low- and lower-middle-income countries.
magnitude: Peering-vs-transit cost savings are linked to lower broadband prices, with the strongest effects in low- and lower-middle-income countries

design: Instrumental variables using historical Eisenhower interstate highway corridors (which fiber-optic routes tend to follow) to instrument for data-center capacity siting, state-level…
authors: Asa Watten, John Bistline, Geoffrey Blanford
title: Have Data Centers Raised Your Electric Bill? Causal Evidence from the United States
data: State-level panel of data center capacity and residential electricity prices, 2015-2024
findings: Using an IV strategy that isolates data-center siting from unobserved local price drivers, a doubling of data-center capacity is found to causally lower residential electricity prices by about 3.5% at a fixed level of demand. The typical residential customer lived in a state where data-center capacity grew 160% between 2019 and 2024, which is estimated to have cut their electricity rates by about 6%. The results reject the hypothesis that data centers shift costs onto residential ratepayers while capturing discounted industrial rates.
magnitude: A doubling of data center capacity causally lowers residential electricity rates by about 3.5%, rejecting a cost-shifting-to-households narrative

design: Ring comparisons around 1,118 geocoded facilities using satellite night-lights, plus a built-versus-announced-but-cancelled near-miss design (43 built vs 49 cancelled hyperscale si…
title: The local economic impact of data centers
data: 1,118 geocoded data-center facilities (341 hyperscale), VIIRS satellite night-time radiance, advertised-salary and new-firm registration panels, school district finance records, residential electricity prices
findings: A carefully designed null result, and a useful corrective to industry impact studies. The physical footprint of a data center is unmistakable — night-time radiance within 1km of an isolated site jumps 38-70 percent at construction start, fading to near zero beyond 5km. But the local economic spillovers are not detectable: advertised salaries and new-firm registrations show no significant increase, with 95 percent confidence intervals ruling out increases above 5.5 percent and 1.6 percent respectively. Rents rise modestly (2-5 percent in synthetic control). School district property-tax revenue rises 16.6 percent and capital outlay per pupil 28.5 percent, but neither survives correction for multiple testing across six fiscal outcomes, and the authors describe them as suggestive rather than robust. Residential electricity prices show no increase. Notably, the paper tests a shift-share instrument similar to that used elsewhere in this literature and rejects it, finding it independently predicts manufacturing and health-sector activity and so violates the exclusion restriction.
magnitude: Capital footprint +38-70% at the parcel, but no detectable wage or firm-entry effect (95% CI upper bounds 5.5% and 1.6%)

design: Cross-country survey of AI adoption in the United States and Europe, linked to industry productivity data
authors: Bick, Blandin, Deming, Fuchs-Schündeln and Jessen
title: Mind the gap: AI adoption in Europe and the U.S.
venue: NBER Working Paper 34995 (forthcoming, Brookings Papers on Economic Activity)
countries: United States and multiple European countries
data: Harmonised cross-country adoption surveys linked to industry-level productivity and employment series
findings: Documents large gaps in AI adoption between the United States and Europe, and across European countries, partly explained by workforce demographics and organisational structure. Firms that actively encourage employees to use AI show markedly higher adoption. Industries with stronger AI adoption show faster productivity growth in both regions, and by a comparable magnitude — but the authors find no clear evidence that industry-level AI adoption is associated with employment changes either way.
magnitude: Large US-Europe adoption gap; adoption correlates with faster industry productivity growth but not with employment change

design: Survey of roughly 6,000 firm executives on AI adoption and expected effects
title: Firm data on AI
data: Executive survey covering approximately 6,000 firms
findings: One of the largest firm-side reads on what managers actually expect from AI, and the expectations are far more modest than the discourse. Sixty-nine percent of surveyed firms report using AI. Over a three-year horizon executives expect AI to raise productivity by 1.4 percent and output by 0.8 percent, and to reduce employment by 0.7 percent. These are stated expectations rather than realised outcomes, but their moderate size is notable against task-level experiments that find double-digit productivity gains, and is closer to the macro estimates in the model-based literature.
magnitude: 69% of firms use AI; executives expect +1.4% productivity, +0.8% output and −0.7% employment over three years

design: Nationally representative firm survey (BTOS AI supplement), firm/function/task-level analysis
authors: Bonney, K., Breaux, C., Dinlersoz, E., Foster, L., Haltiwanger, J., Pande, A.
title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion: Evidence from Firms, Business Functions, and Worker Tasks
venue: US Census Bureau Center for Economic Studies Working Paper CES-26-25
data: 2026 AI supplement to the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS), a large nationally representative firm panel
findings: 18% of firms currently use AI (32% on an employment-weighted basis), rising to 50-60% among very large firms in Information, Professional Services, and Finance. Among adopters, 57% use AI in three or fewer business functions, most often Sales/Marketing (52%), Strategy/Business Development (45%), and IT (41%). Only 23% of firms (41% employment-weighted) apply AI directly to worker tasks, and just 2% of firms report AI-related headcount reductions so far.
magnitude: 18% of US firms use AI (32% employment-weighted); only 2% report AI-related headcount cuts to date

design: Game-theoretic model of data-center operator renewable-certificate/PPA choices plus difference-in-differences using staggered large-language-model releases as natural experiments o…
authors: Dana Golden, Aruna Balasubramanian, Niranjan Balasubramanian
title: Certificates without Electrons? Theory and Evidence on Impacts from AI-Driven Power Demand
data: Novel dataset linking AI model release activity to local grid outcomes (wholesale prices, outage frequency) in PJM zones
findings: Data centers represent about 4.4% of US electricity demand. Using staggered large-language-model releases as natural experiments, wholesale electricity prices rise by up to 25% in treated PJM zones, and outage frequency increases by 0.5-1 additional outages per year near data centers, with impacts scaling with model size. A 'timing wedge' between real-time consumption and annually-averaged renewable energy certificate (REC) attribution means data centers claiming 100% annual REC coverage still degrade grid reliability; behind-the-meter colocation with storage is more effective than RECs alone at mitigating these externalities.
magnitude: Wholesale electricity prices rise up to 25% in PJM zones exposed to data-center load following major AI model releases

design: LLM-based textual analysis of corporate/policy/media disclosures combined with energy-system modeling to project data center electricity footprints and regional grid stress
authors: Danbo Chen, Zijun Zhou, Yongyang Cai, Jiahong Qin, Ani Katchova, Lei Chen
title: Concentrated siting of AI data centers drives regional power-system stress under rising global compute demand
countries: United States, Ireland, Japan, and other major AI-compute hubs
data: Corporate disclosure text analysis (LLM-based) combined with quantitative energy-system modeling for six leading AI firms
findings: More than 90% of projected global AI compute capacity concentrates in North America, Western Europe, and Asia-Pacific. Electricity consumption of six leading AI firms' data centers is projected to rise from about 118 TWh in 2024 to 239-295 TWh by 2030 (roughly 1% of global power demand). A constructed Power Stress Index exceeds critical thresholds (0.25) in Oregon, Virginia, and Ireland, indicating local grid vulnerability, while Texas and Japan show better absorption capacity due to more diversified infrastructure.
magnitude: Six leading AI firms' data center electricity use is projected to roughly double to triple, from 118 TWh (2024) to 239-295 TWh (2030)

design: Difference-in-differences with staggered adoption timing across US data center facility openings
title: The Local Economic Effects of Data Center Entry
venue: SSRN working paper (abbreviated as 'The Local Economic Effects of AI Data Center Entry,' Academy of Management Proceedings, 2026)
data: Staggered-adoption panel of US data center facility openings (Georgia Tech Scheller College of Business) matched to county economic outcomes (employment, wages, establishments, household income, building permits, electricity prices)
findings: Data center activation increases local employment by 3.5%, total wages by 5.0%, business establishments by 4.7%, median household income by 1.9%, and building permits by 16.1% in the longer run (3-year effects are smaller: employment +0.9%, wages +1.1%, establishments +1%), alongside a roughly 5% increase in retail electricity prices for local ratepayers. Effects are heavily concentrated in metropolitan counties (employment +4.1%, wages +5.5%) and are negligible in non-metro/rural counties; Big Tech-owned facilities generate larger local benefits than third-party data centers, and clustered entries amplify gains.
magnitude: Data center entry raises metro-county employment by 4.1% and wages by 5.5%, while rural/non-metro counties see negligible job or wage spillovers

design: Causal/quasi-experimental county-panel analysis of the timing of the first large data-center opening (2008-2024), comparing hyperscale vs. colocation facilities and metro vs.
title: Data Centers and Local Labor Markets (summarized in "New evidence on data center employment effects")
data: Panel of about 770 US data center facilities across 93 counties with their first large facility opening between 2008 and 2024
findings: Total private employment in a county rises 4-5% over the 5-6 years following a large data center's opening, with construction employment up 11% and information-sector employment up 22%; wages rise 3-4%. In a typical county of about 98,000 workers, this translates into roughly 2,000-4,000 additional jobs after six years. Counties that accumulate 4 or more facilities see information-sector employment gains of about 23%. Hyperscale facilities receive far smaller subsidies relative to investment (about 2%) than colocation facilities (about 62%), despite colocation generating smaller local benefits.
magnitude: A county's first large data center raises total private employment by 4-5% and information-sector employment by 22% over 5-6 years, but subsidy generosity is inversely related to facility type's local benefit (colocation facilities get ~62% of investment subsi…

design: Empirical analysis of cyber-insurance broker/policy microdata (adverse selection and screening)
title: Selection and Screening in Cyber Insurance Markets
period: Not precisely specified in verified abstract; recent cyber-i…
data: Microdata from a major cyber-insurance broker on firms' insurance applications, broker use, and policy purchase decisions
findings: Firms with higher underlying cyber risk are more likely both to engage an insurance broker and to purchase cyber coverage, evidence of adverse selection into the market. Insurers appear to manage this risk mainly through coverage caps/sub-limits rather than through risk-based price differentiation, and standard survey-based underwriting questionnaires are only weakly correlated with firms' actual measured cyber risk.
magnitude: Riskier firms self-select into brokered cyber coverage, yet insurer underwriting surveys are only weakly correlated with actual firm risk

design: Archival analysis of newly mandated SEC cybersecurity disclosures in annual reports
title: Mandatory Cybersecurity Disclosure: Early Evidence from 10-K Reports
venue: International Journal of Accounting Information Systems
period: Fiscal years ending on/after December 15, 2023 (first mandat…
data: 10-K cybersecurity risk-management, strategy, and governance disclosures filed by U.S. public companies under the SEC's new mandatory cybersecurity disclosure rule
findings: Provides early archival evidence on how firms are complying with the SEC's 2023 rule requiring annual 10-K disclosure of cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and board governance, and material incident reporting within four business days on Form 8-K Item 1.05, documenting variation in disclosure quality, length, and boilerplate versus substantive content across early adopters.
magnitude: Documents substantial cross-firm variation in the quality and specificity of newly mandated cybersecurity risk disclosures under the SEC's 2023 rule

design: Shift-share IV (fiber-node proximity x Chinese data-center revenue growth; 1980 urban college population share x rest-of-world data-center revenue growth), county-level long differ…
authors: Fernando E. Alvarez, David Argente, Joyce Chow, Diana Van Patten
title: Data Centers and Local Economies in the Age of AI: A Shift-Share Approach
data: 451 Research Datacenter Knowledge Base (12,960+ facilities, 2,700+ providers, 131 countries) matched to County Business Patterns, IRS Statistics of Income, FHFA house price index, and EIA Form 861 electricity prices
findings: A one-log-point increase in cumulative data-center revenue in a county raises total employment by 3.9%, data-processing employment by 29.4%, establishments by 6.2%, house prices by 17.7%, and electricity prices by 0.9% by 2020 (all significant at 1%); tax returns, adjusted gross income, and wages also rise (5.9%, 8.2%, and 5.9% respectively), though annual payroll responds less robustly. First-stage F-statistics range from 786 to 907. The employment and electricity-price effects weaken and lose significance once state fixed effects are added.
magnitude: Data center revenue growth raises county electricity prices by 0.9% and house prices by 17.7%, with total employment up 3.9% (2SLS, 2020 horizon)

design: Difference-in-differences around the 2019 FTC/YouTube COPPA settlement
authors: Garrett A. Johnson, Tesary Lin, Liang Zhong, James C. Cooper
title: COPPAcalypse? The YouTube Settlement's Impact on Kids' Content
data: YouTube channel- and video-level data on content production and monetization for child-directed content, before and after the FTC's 2019 COPPA settlement restricted personalized advertising on kids' content
findings: After YouTube's 2019 COPPA settlement eliminated targeted advertising and most data collection on child-directed content, monetization for kids' content creators fell sharply, and the platform saw a shift in the volume and mix of child-directed content produced, illustrating how privacy rules that cut off behavioral advertising revenue can reshape content-creator supply incentives on a two-sided platform.
magnitude: Removing targeted ads from child-directed content after the COPPA settlement reduced monetization and reshaped kids' content supply on YouTube

design: Difference-in-differences using a novel linked database of hospital ransomware attacks and Medicare claims
authors: Hannah T. Neprash, Claire McGlave, Sayeh Nikpay
title: Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients
venue: American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, Vol. 18
data: Original database of hospital ransomware attacks linked to Medicare fee-for-service claims data, 2016-2021
findings: Ransomware attacks decrease hospital patient volume by 17-24% during the initial attack week, with volumes recovering within about three weeks. Among patients already hospitalized when an attack begins, in-hospital mortality rises by 34-38% (roughly 3 in 100 hospitalized Medicare patients die in normal times, versus about 4 in 100 during an attack). The authors estimate ransomware attacks killed between 42 and 67 Medicare patients from 2016-2021, with the true toll across all payers likely higher.
magnitude: In-hospital mortality rises 34-38% for patients already admitted when a ransomware attack hits; hospital volume falls 17-24% in the first week

design: Bank-level panel analysis of instant-payment-driven fintech competition exposure
title: Fintech Competition and Banks' Shrinking Margins in Brazil
data: Brazilian bank-level regulatory data on lending rates, net interest margins, and fintech/Pix-driven competition exposure
findings: A one-standard-deviation increase in fintech competition exposure (facilitated by Pix and open-finance reforms) is associated with a 3.7 percentage-point reduction in average commercial-bank lending rates. Between 2018 and 2024, fintech competition is estimated to have lowered average bank lending rates by 2.7 percentage points and compressed net interest margins by 0.9 percentage points, even as banks' operational efficiency improved.
magnitude: Fintech/Pix competition lowered Brazilian bank lending rates by 2.7 percentage points, 2018-2024

design: multi-regional input-output (MRIO) analysis of embodied emissions
authors: Janna Axenbeck, Stefanie Kunkel, Joris Blain, Francis Charpentier
title: Between 2010 and 2021, global emissions from digital technologies were largely obscured in greenhouse gas emission accounting standards
data: Global multi-regional input-output tables covering hardware, IT-services, and communications sectors
findings: Using global input-output analysis, finds digital industries (hardware, IT services, telecom) generated about 4.1% of global GHG emissions in 2021, with 77%-87% of these emissions occurring upstream in supply chains rather than in direct operational electricity use. About 42% of digital-sector emissions are embedded within non-digital industries' outputs, meaning standard GHG accounting frameworks obscure the true scale and location of digital emissions.
magnitude: Digital industries generated ~4.1% of global GHG emissions in 2021, mostly hidden upstream in supply chains

design: National-accounts-style measurement framework with quality adjustment for API price declines and algorithmic progress
title: Measuring the AI economy
data: AI compute spending, inference and training activity, API pricing series, data-center capacity
findings: An attempt to put the AI build-out into national-accounts terms, and a caution about how much the answer depends on quality adjustment. Nominal AI compute spending grew more than 140 percent per year in both 2024 and 2025, and raw compute capacity more than 200 percent per year. Once output is quality-adjusted for falling API prices and algorithmic progress, measured AI output growth exceeds 2,000 percent per year and quality-adjusted AI GDP growth exceeds 2,500 percent. These rates are from a very small base and are a statement about measurement, not about aggregate growth.
magnitude: Nominal AI compute spending +140%/year; quality-adjusted AI output +2,000%/year, from a very small base

design: Large-scale randomized rollout of a digital agricultural trading platform (SMS-based bid/ask matching) at the sub-county level
authors: Lauren Falcao Bergquist, Craig McIntosh, Meredith Startz
title: Search Costs, Intermediation, and Trade: Experimental Evidence from Ugandan Agricultural Markets
venue: Yale Economic Growth Center Discussion Paper No. 1126
data: RCT across 110 sub-counties (11 districts, ~14% of Uganda's surface area) of the Kudu SMS-based trading platform, reaching ~1,000 buyers, 1,411 farmers, 902 traders, and 171 commission agents; platform logged 23,768 asks ($42m) and 30,499 bids ($65m), yielding 1,306 verified sales moving ~8,000 tons
findings: The platform cut fixed trade costs by roughly one-fifth and increased trade flows by about 7% between treated markets (1% market-wide), narrowing maize price dispersion by about 6-11%. Gains concentrated among larger traders able to exploit new arbitrage opportunities, with benefits passing through to farmgate prices (up to 12% higher in previously low-price markets), even though only about 4% of treated farmers directly completed a trade on the platform themselves.
magnitude: Digital trading platform cut fixed trade costs ~20% and raised inter-market trade ~7%, though only 4% of farmers directly transacted on it

design: Difference-in-differences comparing EU vs. non-EU Google Maps search/traffic around the Digital Markets Act's self-preferencing ban
title: Is Competition Only One Click Away? The Digital Markets Act's Impact on Google Maps
period: Around the DMA's 2024 self-preferencing compliance deadline
data: Search and click/traffic data for online mapping services, comparing EU markets (subject to the DMA's ban on Google self-preferencing Maps in search results) with non-EU markets
findings: After the DMA required Google to stop self-preferencing Google Maps in search results, search queries for maps and traffic to Google Maps increased by more than 21% in the EU relative to non-EU markets, indicating that removing self-preferencing measurably increased user search/switching activity and, by implication, competitors' visibility in map-related search results.
magnitude: Ending Google's self-preferencing of Maps under the DMA increased EU map-related search queries and Google Maps traffic by more than 21%

design: Event-study analysis using unemployment insurance records, LinkedIn cohort tracking, and syllabus text analysis
authors: Morgan R. Frank, Alireza Javadian Sabet, Lisa Simon, Sarah H. Bana, Renzhe Yu
title: AI-Exposed Jobs Deteriorated Before ChatGPT
data: Monthly US unemployment insurance records by occupation/location; millions of LinkedIn profiles tracking graduate hiring cohorts; millions of university syllabi records measuring curricular AI exposure
findings: Unemployment risk in AI-exposed occupations began rising in early 2022, months before ChatGPT's November 2022 release, and new-graduate cohorts from 2021 onward entered AI-exposed jobs at lower rates than earlier cohorts, with the gap opening before ChatGPT. After ChatGPT's release, graduates with more AI-relevant coursework experienced higher first-job pay and shorter job searches, suggesting curricular AI exposure became an asset even as occupational AI exposure became a risk.
magnitude: AI-exposed occupations' unemployment risk began rising in early 2022, predating ChatGPT's launch by roughly nine months

design: Facility-level emissions accounting combined with the AP4 integrated assessment model and EPA social cost of carbon
title: Measuring the Impact of Data Centers in the United States Economy: Monetary Damage from Air Pollution and Greenhouse Gas Emissions
data: Facility-level data for approximately 2,800 US data centers combined with electricity grid emissions data, the AP4 integrated assessment model, and the social cost of carbon
findings: This paper quantifies the environmental externalities associated with electricity consumption by data centers in the United States, focusing on damages from local air pollution and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Using facility-level data for approximately 2,800 operational data centers in 2025, combined with electricity grid characteristics and emissions data, the analysis estimates pollution impacts through the AP4 integrated assessment model and applies the social cost of carbon for GHG valuation. Results indicate that data centers consume roughly 250 TWh of electricity—about 5–6% of U.S. generation—and generate approximately $25 billion in gross external damages (GED), with a range of $10–$33 billion. These damages are highly geographically concentrated, with Texas and Virginia accounting for 30% of the national total. While GED comprises about 5% of industry GDP, this ratio varies widely across states, exceeding GDP in some regions. Planned data center expansion could increase electricity demand and associated damages by up to 85% in the near term. Despite these environmental costs, preliminary comparisons suggest that the damages attributable to AI-related energy use are small relative to potential productivity gains.
magnitude: US data centers caused about $25 billion per year in gross external pollution and climate damages in 2025

design: Hourly, unit-level least-cost dispatch model of continental US wholesale electricity markets, with projections under high- and moderate-utilization data-center build-out scenarios
authors: Owen Kay, Robert Reaser, Reid Taylor
title: Processing Power: The Effect of Data Centers on Wholesale Electricity Markets
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Working Paper 2606
period: current market data with projections through 2028
data: Hourly unit-level dispatch modeling of continental US wholesale electricity markets linked to data center load corridors
findings: Existing data centers have already raised average wholesale electricity prices by an estimated 3-5% nationwide, with larger effects concentrated in regions hosting major data center corridors. Under a high-utilization build-out scenario continuing through 2028, the model projects wholesale prices could rise by roughly 50%; under a more moderate build-out scenario, the projected increase is closer to 20%.
magnitude: Data centers have already raised nationwide wholesale electricity prices by 3-5%, with a projected rise of up to 50% by 2028 under high-growth build-out scenarios

design: Nationally representative survey, American Trends Panel
title: The Gender Gap in AI in the US
data: Survey of 5,119 US adults via Pew's American Trends Panel
findings: Overall chatbot adoption has converged by gender (49% of both men and women report ever using an AI chatbot), but usage intensity and perceived value have not: men use chatbots daily more often (27% vs. 20%), report greater productivity benefits (35% vs. 25%), and report more familiarity with AI (55% vs. 41% 'heard a lot'). Women are twice as likely as men to expect AI to hurt them personally (33% vs. 17%) and are more likely to think AI is advancing too quickly (68% vs. 58%).
magnitude: US chatbot adoption has equalized by gender (49% vs 49%), but women report 10pp lower perceived productivity benefit and much greater concern

design: Input-output economic contribution modelling commissioned by an industry trade association
authors: PwC for the Data Center Coalition
title: Economic contributions of data centers in the United States
data: Industry financial data and employment statistics run through an input-output contribution model, national and state level
findings: The most widely cited industry estimate of the data-center sector's economic footprint, and a useful contrast with the quasi-experimental local studies in this repository. It reports a contribution of $926.9 billion to US GDP in 2024, 5.5 million jobs supported, and $204.4 billion in federal, state and local tax revenue, up from $727 billion and 4.7 million jobs on 2023 data. These are gross contribution figures from an input-output model commissioned by the industry, not causal estimates: they count activity associated with the sector rather than activity that would not have occurred otherwise, and they should not be compared like-for-like with the near-zero local spillovers that credible quasi-experimental designs recover.
magnitude: $926.9 billion gross GDP contribution and 5.5 million jobs supported in 2024 — a contribution accounting figure, not a causal estimate

design: Neural-network model trained on US data center facility siting patterns to forecast development at fine geographic resolution
authors: Rui Du, Xiaojin Sun, Siqi Zheng
title: Bits and Mortar: The Microspatial Economics of Data Centers
data: US data center facility-level siting data, 2010-2024
findings: Hyperscale cloud operators and third-party (colocation) operators reveal distinct siting priorities: hyperscalers emphasize power-grid reliability and available transmission infrastructure, while third-party operators prioritize power availability and cost above other factors. Projections through 2030 indicate that rising AI compute demand will strain existing data center regions, but distributed power generation and renewable-energy expansion could enable new growth in previously marginal locations, indicating that energy policy is becoming a first-order driver of data-center location decisions.
magnitude: Hyperscale and third-party data center operators reveal systematically different siting priorities (grid reliability vs. power cost), with energy policy now a first-order determinant of where new capacity locates

design: Synthetic control
findings: Estimate the impact of Value Added Tax exemptions on smartphone penetration in Colombia using the synthetic control method. Colombia announced a VAT exemption on low-cost mobile handsets in late 2016 and implemented the change in 2017. The study finds that smartphone penetration rates rose to 66.8 % by the end of 2021, an increase of 7.6 percentage points and +12.8 % over the 59.2 % level of its synthetic counterpart. Additionally, a preliminary cost-benefit analysis suggests that the broader economic gains from increased smartphone penetration could plausibly offset the VAT revenue losses over time.

design: Compilation of benchmark, investment, adoption, and infrastructure indicators
authors: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI)
title: The 2026 AI Index Report
countries: Global, with country-level comparisons (US, China, South Korea, others)
data: Compiled global data on AI benchmarks, corporate investment, organizational adoption surveys, data-center counts, and patenting
findings: Global corporate AI investment reached $581.7 billion in 2025 (+130% year-over-year), with US private AI investment of $285.9 billion more than 23 times China's $12.4 billion. Organizational AI adoption reached 88%, and the US hosts 5,427 data centers (more than 10 times any other country) while nearly all leading AI chips are fabricated by a single Taiwanese foundry (TSMC), underscoring compute concentration risk. The report also flags that responsible-AI reporting (safety evaluations, bias audits) lags far behind capability growth.
magnitude: US private AI investment ($285.9B) was 23x China's ($12.4B) in 2025, and the US hosts 10x more data centers than any other country

design: Financial-economics analysis of data center capital structures, financing vehicles, and systemic-risk exposures
title: Financing the AI Buildout
data: Hyperscaler capex projections, Morgan Stanley Research financing estimates, and a detailed capital-structure case study of Meta's Hyperion data center/Blue Owl 'Beignet' joint venture
findings: The AI buildout implies roughly $8.2 trillion in cumulative data-center investment (facilities, power infrastructure, and IT equipment) for about 200 GW of new US capacity by 2032, averaging about 2.8% of GDP per year over 2025-2032 -- exceeding the railroad boom (2.4%/year, 1865-1890), electrification (1.1%/year), the interstate highway system (1.6%/year), and the 1996-2003 telecom/fiber buildout (0.8%/year). An estimated $2.9 trillion is needed for hyperscaler compute alone through 2028, over half externally financed via private credit, corporate debt, and structured finance, with asset-level leverage of 70-90%; in one example, Meta sold an 80% equity stake in its 2-gigawatt, $30 billion Hyperion data center to Blue Owl for $2.5 billion, and the resulting joint venture raised $27 billion in A+-rated debt (the largest investment-grade corporate debt issuance in US history), implying about 90% leverage on the underlying assets.
magnitude: The AI data-center buildout implies about $8.2 trillion in investment and 2.8% of GDP per year through 2032 -- exceeding the 19th-century railroad boom -- financed at 70-90% leverage

design: Calibrated two-sector open-economy asset-pricing and growth model, disciplined by observed corporate capital expenditure
title: What investment data implies about the AI transition
data: Capital expenditure of the five largest US technology firms, national accounts, asset-price series
findings: Reads the AI transition off what firms are actually spending rather than off task-exposure indices. The five largest US technology firms spent $380 billion on capital expenditure in 2025, forecast to roughly double in 2026. Calibrating a boom that raises AI-sector productivity by a factor of about 2.7, the model implies additional cumulative GDP growth of 5 to 58 percentage points by 2030 — an enormous range that is itself the paper's main message about uncertainty — with the AI share of the economy running between 8 and 39 percent. In financial markets the risk-free rate rises by about half a percentage point and the equity premium by about 3 percentage points.
magnitude: $380 billion big-tech capex in 2025; implied cumulative GDP gain of 5 to 58 percentage points by 2030

design: Flagship report framing (concept note) with cross-country labor-market AI-exposure analysis
title: World Development Report 2026: Decoding AI (Artificial Intelligence for Development)
data: Cross-country task/occupational exposure analysis spanning 135 countries, plus case evidence on AI applications in credit access, education, and health
findings: The report frames AI as a general-purpose technology whose development impact depends on complementary digital infrastructure and institutions; it finds labor-market exposure to AI varies significantly across the 135 countries studied by job/task composition. It highlights potential for developing countries to 'leapfrog' legacy constraints (e.g., AI-based credit scoring substituting for thin credit bureaus) but warns of risks of AI-driven inequality and technological dependency without governance reforms.
magnitude: Cross-country AI labor-exposure analysis across 135 countries frames AI as a general-purpose technology requiring complementary institutions

design: Hedonic wage regressions on global online job postings using a standardized digital-skills taxonomy
authors: Yan Liu, Antonio Martins Neto, Saloni Khurana, Juan Manuel Porras
title: Click, Code, Earn: The Returns to Digital Skills
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11313
data: 67 million online job postings from 29 countries (2021-2024), coded with a new standardized digital-skills taxonomy (basic, intermediate, advanced/AI)
findings: Requiring at least one digital skill raises advertised wages by 1.6% on average, but the premium is roughly 5x larger in poorer countries: 7.5% in low- and middle-income countries versus 1.3% in high-income countries. Each additional digital skill adds 2.6% to wages in developing economies versus 0.5% in wealthy ones. Generative AI skills carry the largest premiums: 7-9% in technical occupations and 25-36% in non-technical professional roles.
magnitude: Digital-skill wage premium is ~7.5% in LMICs vs ~1.3% in high-income countries

design: Quantitative projection of direct water withdrawal for US data-center cooling under current vs. improving water-use-intensity scenarios, with valuation of required new water-system…
authors: Yuelin Han, Pengfei Li, Adam Wierman, Shaolei Ren
title: Small Bottle, Big Pipe: Quantifying and Addressing the Impact of Data Centers on Public Water Systems
data: US data-center water-use-intensity estimates combined with municipal water-system peak-capacity benchmarks (e.g., New York City's water supply)
findings: If 2024 data-center water-use intensity persists, US data centers could require 697-1,451 million gallons per day (MGD) of new water-system capacity by 2030 -- comparable to roughly half to nearly all of New York City's average daily water supply (~1,000 MGD) -- valued at $10 billion, rising to as much as $58 billion in a high-growth scenario. Under a 10%-per-year efficiency-improvement scenario, needed capacity falls to 227-604 MGD. Impacts are highly concentrated in host communities' local water systems, and the authors recommend peak-water-use reporting and 'Water Capacity Neutral' commitments alongside coordinated water-power planning.
magnitude: New US water-system capacity needed for data centers by 2030 is valued at $10-58 billion, with peak demand potentially rivaling New York City's entire water supply

design: 2x2 factorial cluster-randomized controlled trial, village-level randomization
authors: Abate, G.T., Boukaka, S., Deutschmann, J., Bernard, T., Spielman, D. (IFPRI/University of Chicago/University of Bordeaux…
title: Improving Smallholder Agriculture with Generative AI: The Impact of Farmer.Chat in Kenya
data: 600 villages, approximately 3,000 farmer observations; cross-randomized Farmer.Chat AI chatbot access and a video-testimonial nudge, with embedded onboarding/feedback-group sub-treatments
findings: This is one of the first RCTs designed to produce causal evidence on generative AI agricultural extension, measuring impacts on extension access, knowledge and adoption of recommended practices, farmer agency, productivity, income, and food security. As of the July 2026 registry status, the trial is ongoing and no impact results have been published yet.
magnitude: First causal RCT of a generative-AI farm-advisory chatbot at scale; results not yet available (ongoing through March 2027)

design: Task-based macroeconomic model; Hulten's theorem decomposition of automation exposure and cost savings
title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
venue: Economic Policy, Vol. 40, Issue 121 (also NBER Working Paper 32487)
data: Task-exposure estimates and cost-savings calibration applied to a Hulten's-theorem style growth-accounting framework
findings: Under plausible calibrations of task exposure and cost savings, AI's total factor productivity gains over the next decade are estimated at only 0.53-0.66%, implying annual TFP growth of about 0.064% -- far below the much larger productivity boosts (1.5% p.a. or more) projected by Goldman Sachs and McKinsey. The paper argues AI excels at structured, codifiable tasks but has limited near-term impact on complex judgment-based tasks that dominate GDP.
magnitude: AI raises US TFP by only about 0.66% cumulatively over 10 years (~0.06%/year), far below Wall Street forecasts

design: Difference-in-differences on linked survey and matched employer-employee administrative data
title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI (previously circulated as 'Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects')
venue: NBER Working Paper 33777 / Becker Friedman Institute Working Paper
data: Two large-scale AI-chatbot adoption surveys (late 2023 and 2024) covering 25,000 workers and 7,000 workplaces in 11 exposed occupations, linked to Danish matched employer-employee administrative data
findings: Despite near-universal employer adoption of chatbot initiatives in exposed occupations, the study finds precisely estimated null effects of AI chatbots on earnings and recorded hours at both worker and workplace level, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT's release. Estimated time savings from chatbot use are only about 3%. Null results are robust across intensive users, early adopters, high-investment workplaces, and early-career jobs; employers instead absorbed AI through task reorganization rather than pay or hours changes.
magnitude: Earnings/hours effects ruled out above 2%; time savings ~3%, two years post-ChatGPT

design: Systematic review (SPIDER search strategy, PRISMA screening) of RCTs of skills-training programs
authors: Bernd Beber, Tabea Lakemann, Regina Schnars, Jann Lay
title: Employment Effects of Skills Trainings in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review of Recent Randomized Controlled Trials
data: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials evaluating employment effects of skills-training programs, 2019-2024
findings: The review finds a shift toward a more optimistic assessment of skills-training employment effects relative to the pessimistic pre-2019 literature (e.g., McKenzie's earlier reviews), with most recent SSA RCTs showing measurable improvements in employment outcomes. The authors attribute part of the improvement to better-targeted, market-linked program designs rather than generic vocational courses.
magnitude: Majority of 2019-2024 SSA skills-training RCTs reviewed show positive employment effects, reversing earlier pessimism

design: Structural bidder-valuation model of spectrum auctions with counterfactual auction-design simulation
title: Spectrum Allocation to Public Operators: A Structural Analysis of Set-Asides versus Subsidies in Indian Telecom Auctions
data: Indian telecom spectrum-auction bidding data used to estimate a structural model of bidder valuations, with counterfactual auction-design simulations
findings: Compares policies for allocating spectrum to public-sector telecom operators, estimating that allowing the public operator to bid competitively without a subsidy raises expected auction revenue by about 7% relative to set-aside/subsidy schemes, and that location-targeted subsidies outperform nationwide subsidies for achieving coverage goals at lower fiscal cost.
magnitude: Letting the public operator bid without a subsidy raises expected Indian spectrum-auction revenue by about 7%; location-targeted subsidies dominate nationwide ones

design: Computable general equilibrium model (IMF-ENV) with firm and sector data, projected to 2030
authors: Bogmans, Gomez-Gonzalez, Ganpurev, Melina, Pescatori and Thube
title: Power hungry: how AI will drive energy demand
data: US firm and sector electricity cost and output data 2019-2023, global energy and emissions accounts
findings: Puts a price on the electricity that AI compute will draw. US AI-producing sectors grew at nearly triple the rate of the broader private non-farm business sector, and electricity costs for vertically integrated AI companies nearly doubled between 2019 and 2023. Under a scenario of constrained renewable growth and limited transmission expansion, the model projects that AI-driven data-center growth raises US electricity prices by 8.6 percent and raises US and global carbon emissions by 5.5 percent and 1.2 percent respectively under current policies. The transmission constraint, not generation, does most of the work.
magnitude: +8.6% US electricity prices and +5.5% US emissions from AI data-center growth under constrained-infrastructure scenarios

design: Staggered rollout of generative AI tool across customer support agents (difference-in-differences)
authors: Brynjolfsson, E., Li, D., Raymond, L.R.
title: Generative AI at Work
venue: Quarterly Journal of Economics, Vol. 140, Issue 2 (also NBER WP 31161)
data: Administrative productivity data for 5,179 customer support agents at a Fortune 500 software firm, before/after staggered access to a GPT-based conversational assistant
findings: Access to the AI assistant increased average agent productivity (issues resolved per hour) by 14%, with gains concentrated among less experienced and lower-skilled workers, who improved by around 34%; the most experienced agents saw minimal or slightly negative effects on speed/quality. The tool also improved customer sentiment and reduced employee turnover, consistent with the AI diffusing best practices from high performers to novices.
magnitude: 14% average productivity gain from generative AI assistance; 34% gain for novice workers versus near-zero for top performers

design: Long-run follow-up of RCT using 10 years of administrative data, 531 rural schools
authors: Cueto, Beuermann, Cristia, Malamud, and Pardo
title: Laptops in the long run: Evidence from the one laptop per child program in rural Peru
data: Administrative records on academic performance and grade progression over 10 years for students in 531 randomized rural primary schools (original OLPC RCT)
findings: Ten years after randomized laptop distribution, there are no significant long-run effects on academic performance or grade progression when following schools over time, and no significant effects on educational attainment when following individual students over time -- confirming that the short-run null effects on learning outcomes persist rather than being merely delayed.
magnitude: No detectable long-run effects on learning or educational attainment 10 years after randomized OLPC laptop distribution across 531 schools

design: Randomized controlled trial of a six-week generative-AI chatbot tutoring pilot
authors: Martin E. De Simone, Federico Tiberti, Wuraola Mosuro, Federico Manolio, Maria Barron, Eliot Dikoru
title: From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Transforming Learning in Nigeria, One Prompt at a Time
data: Randomized evaluation of a generative-AI chatbot tutoring pilot (English, AI knowledge, digital literacy) in an Edo State secondary school
findings: The six-week AI chatbot tutoring pilot raised learning outcomes by about 0.3 standard deviations, described as equivalent to nearly two years of typical learning gained in six weeks, outperforming roughly 80% of RCT-evaluated education interventions in the developing world. Girls gained more than boys, each additional day of attendance was associated with further gains, and treated students also scored better on end-of-year exams covering material beyond the intervention.
magnitude: 0.3 SD learning gain in six weeks, equivalent to roughly two years of typical learning

design: Meta-analysis of RCT intent-to-treat estimates across active labor market policy (ALMP) types
authors: Eduardo Levy Yeyati, Martin Montane, Luca Sartorio, Alfonso Gauna
title: What Works for Active Labor Market Policies? A Meta-Analysis of RCT Findings
countries: Mix of countries across 73 RCTs (mostly since 2014)
data: 102 ALMP interventions drawn from 73 RCTs; 668 intent-to-treat coefficients on employment and earnings outcomes
findings: Median earnings gains relative to control were 16.7% for wage subsidies, 16.5% for entrepreneurship/independent-worker support, and 7.7% for vocational training, versus a negligible effect for employment services; median employment gains were 11%, 11%, and 6.7% respectively. Only about one-third of the 668 estimated coefficients were positive and statistically significant. Individualized coaching, monetary incentives, and sector-specific targeting were associated with larger effects for vocational training.
magnitude: Vocational training raises earnings by a median 7.7% vs 16.7% for wage subsidies; only ~1/3 of ALMP estimates are significant

design: High-frequency administrative payroll panel, difference-in-differences controlling for firm-level shocks
authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen
title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab / SIEPR Working Paper
data: Monthly administrative payroll records from ADP, the largest US payroll-software provider, by detailed occupation
findings: Early-career workers (ages 22-25) in the most AI-exposed occupations experienced a 16% relative decline in employment since generative AI's widespread adoption, controlling for firm-level shocks, while employment for more experienced workers in the same occupations held stable or grew. Adjustment occurred mainly through headcount rather than compensation, and declines concentrated in occupations where AI automates rather than augments tasks.
magnitude: 16% relative employment decline for 22-25 year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations

design: Randomized field experiment with three arms (no AI / GPT-4 / GPT-4 plus prompt training)
authors: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Edward McFowland III, Ethan Mollick, Hila Lifshitz-Assaf, Katherine Kellogg, Saran Rajendran, Lisa…
title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
data: 758 BCG consultants (~7% of individual-contributor consultants) randomized across AI-access conditions on a realistic consulting task battery
findings: Inside the 'jagged frontier' of tasks AI handles well, consultants using GPT-4 completed 12.2% more tasks, worked 25.1% faster, and were rated 33.9% higher quality by human graders than the control group. Outside the frontier, on tasks beyond AI's current capability, AI users were 19% less likely to produce correct solutions, and elite consultants using AI produced less varied (more homogeneous) outputs.
magnitude: Inside frontier: +12.2% tasks completed, 25.1% faster, quality +33.9%; outside frontier: -19% correct-solution rate

design: 3-arm randomized controlled experiment (textbook-only vs. restricted AI tutor vs. unrestricted AI tutor)
authors: Fischer, M., Rau, H.A., Rilke, R.M.
title: AI Tutoring Enhances Student Learning Without Crowding Out Effort
data: 334 university students preparing for an incentivized exam, randomized to textbook-only, restricted AI-tutor access (after initial independent reading), or unrestricted AI-tutor access
findings: Unrestricted AI tutor access improved test performance by 0.23 SD versus the control group and by 0.21 SD versus restricted access. Benefits were largest for students with lower baseline knowledge and stronger self-regulation; unrestricted access did not crowd out study effort, contradicting fears that free AI access breeds over-reliance. A high-income-country comparison point for the developing-country AI-tutoring RCTs above.
magnitude: Unrestricted AI-tutor access raised exam performance by 0.23 SD without reducing student effort

design: Tracking and tabulation of state/local subsidy deals and official tax-exemption fiscal notes across major US data center projects
authors: Good Jobs First (original per-job subsidy analysis by Kasia Tarczynska, 2016; state revenue-loss estimates from the orga…
title: Cloudy with a Loss of Spending Control: How Data Centers Are Endangering State Budgets (part of an ongoing series building on the organization's 2016 'Money Lost to the Cloud' analysis)
period: 2016 original per-job analysis; state fiscal-note data throu…
data: State/local economic-development subsidy deal tracking and official state fiscal-note projections of sales-tax-exemption revenue losses across 32 states with data-center tax-incentive programs
findings: Good Jobs First's original tracking (2016) found the 11 largest publicly disclosed data-center subsidy megadeals averaged $1.95 million in public subsidy per permanent job (e.g., Apple's North Carolina deal was $321 million in incentives for 50 permanent jobs, or $6.4 million per job). Its 2025 update finds at least 10 of 32 states with data-center tax-incentive programs each lose more than $100 million per year: Texas lost $1.015 billion in 2025 (up 669% from a $130 million estimate made in February 2023), Virginia lost $732.8 million in 2024, Illinois lost $370.6 million in 2023 (up 3,600% since 2020), and Georgia lost $296 million in 2025; 12 states provide no public disclosure of these revenue losses at all.
magnitude: Major US data center subsidy deals have averaged $1.95 million in public subsidy per permanent job, while Texas's annual tax-exemption cost rose 669% in 23 months to over $1 billion

design: Nationally representative household surveys across low- and middle-income countries
title: The Mobile Gender Gap Report 2025
data: Nationally representative household surveys on mobile phone and mobile internet ownership/use across LMICs
findings: Women in LMICs are 14% less likely than men to use mobile internet, and roughly 885 million women remain unconnected to mobile internet. The gender gap in mobile ownership is 8 points and in smartphone ownership 14 points; these gaps were unchanged in 2024, indicating stalled progress. Closing the digital gender gap is estimated to be worth $1.5 trillion in additional global GDP -- a foundational access constraint underlying gender gaps in AI use specifically.
magnitude: 885 million women in LMICs remain unconnected to mobile internet; the usage gender gap (14%) was unchanged in 2024

design: Systematic review/synthesis of causal literature (153 studies)
title: The Economic Impact of Internet Connectivity in Developing Countries
countries: Cross-country synthesis, primarily Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Latin America
data: Meta-review of 153 empirical studies using RCTs, natural experiments, and quasi-experimental designs on internet/mobile connectivity in developing countries
findings: Synthesizes evidence that internet connectivity raises firm entry, productivity, and exports; shifts workers into higher-productivity, higher-skill jobs and out of subsistence agriculture; and increases access to information, credit, and markets. Also documents negative effects via misinformation, political polarization, and reduced trust in government, and stresses that gains are highly dependent on complementary infrastructure and human capital.
magnitude: Across 153 reviewed studies, internet expansion consistently raises employment/productivity in connected areas, but gains concentrate among more-educated workers and larger firms

design: Spatial/geographic regression using distance to pre-2007 AI innovation hubs
authors: Hunt, J., Cockburn, I.M., Bessen, J.
title: Is Distance from Innovation a Barrier to the Adoption of Artificial Intelligence?
data: AI academic publication locations merged with Burning Glass online vacancy data (2007-2019) at the commuting-zone level
findings: A commuting zone an additional 200km from the nearest pre-2007 AI hotspot experiences 17% lower growth in AI jobs' share of vacancies. The effect is driven by distance from AI academic research (not patents) and is partly explained by state borders impeding migration and tacit knowledge transfer, affecting both core AI research roles and roles that merely apply AI across industries.
magnitude: Each extra 200km from an AI hotspot is associated with 17% lower growth in local AI-job vacancy share

design: Energy-system demand modeling and scenario analysis
title: Energy and AI: Energy Demand from AI
countries: Global, with country-level breakdowns (US, China, EU)
data: Global electricity demand and data-center capacity data with scenario modeling to 2030
findings: Data centers consumed about 536 TWh in 2025 (roughly 2% of global electricity), with data-center electricity demand growing 17% in 2025 while AI-focused data-center demand alone surged 50%. Global data-center electricity consumption could roughly double to about 1,065 TWh by 2030. Data centers currently account for just over 1% of global electricity demand and 0.5% of CO2 emissions, projected to reach about 1-1.4% of emissions by 2030; renewable energy is growing about 22%/year and could meet nearly half of incremental demand.
magnitude: AI-focused data-center electricity demand grew 50% in 2025 alone; total data-center demand could double to ~1,065 TWh by 2030

design: Bottom-up geospatial cost model selecting the least-cost technology (urban fibre, rural fixed wireless, remote satellite) area by area
title: Connecting humanity action blueprint: advancing sustainable, affordable and innovative solutions
countries: Global, with emphasis on least-developed countries
data: Geospatial population and household distribution matched against mobile coverage and fibre network maps, operator cost data, expert advisory group
findings: The authoritative costing of what universal connectivity would actually take, and a useful denominator for every impact estimate in this repository. In 2024, 2.6 billion people remained unconnected, down from about 3 billion in 2020. Reaching universal meaningful connectivity at 20 Mbps or better by 2030 is costed at $2.6 to $2.8 trillion. The digital infrastructure component alone — last-mile networks, data centres, IXPs and backbone, plus operating expenditure — is $1.46 to $1.71 trillion, roughly half the total. The affordability gap is about $983 billion, the digital-skills gap about $152 billion for the 1.2 billion people needing basic training, and the policy and regulatory gap only about $0.6 billion globally, which is a striking cost-effectiveness contrast.
magnitude: $2.6-2.8 trillion to connect everyone by 2030; the policy and regulatory component is just $0.6 billion of it

design: High-level investment-gap estimate produced with development finance institutions
authors: International Telecommunication Union and Boston Consulting Group
title: Digital infrastructure investment initiative: closing the digital infrastructure investment gap by 2030
venue: ITU white paper, with six development finance institutions
data: Operator and DFI investment data, connectivity gap modelling
findings: Estimates that closing the global connectivity gap by 2030 would cost approximately $1.6 trillion. At the time of analysis 33 percent of the world's population was offline, rising to 54 percent in low- and lower-middle-income countries. Five cost drivers are identified: urban fixed-broadband expansion, rural wireless expansion, roughly 1.7 million kilometres of backbone extension, data-centre capacity in lower-income countries, and high-performance data-centre capacity in upper-middle-income countries. The inclusion of compute capacity as a connectivity cost driver is a notable shift from earlier connectivity costings.
magnitude: $1.6 trillion to close the digital infrastructure gap by 2030; 54% of people in low- and lower-middle-income countries are offline

design: Event study of bank stock returns, loans, and deposits around data breach announcements
title: Data Breach Announcement Effect on Bank Loans, Deposits, and Stock Performance
period: Not precisely specified in verified abstract; recent bank da…
data: Bank-level data breach announcements matched to stock returns, deposit flows, and loan growth for affected banks
findings: Data breach announcements at banks are associated with negative stock market reactions and measurable effects on subsequent deposit-taking and lending activity, indicating that cybersecurity incidents impose a customer-trust cost on financial institutions beyond direct remediation expenses, consistent with depositors and borrowers reacting to perceived operational and reputational risk.
magnitude: Bank data breaches trigger negative stock reactions and subsequent disruption to deposit and loan growth

design: Panel of high-frequency CPU utilization data with a structural learning model of within-firm productivity dynamics after cloud adoption
authors: James M. Brand, Mert Demirer, Connor Finucane, Avner Kreps
title: Firm Productivity and Learning with Digital Technologies: Evidence from Cloud Computing
region: not specified (large cloud provider's client base)
data: High-frequency CPU utilization data for nearly 100,000 firms using cloud infrastructure
findings: Firms improve cloud computing productivity by 33% in the first year after adoption and reach a stable productivity level only after four years. Faster learning among initially less-efficient firms narrows productivity dispersion across firms by 60% over time, though substantial heterogeneity persists even after ten years. Productivity gains occur mainly within individual divisions of a firm, with minimal knowledge transfer across divisions of the same firm.
magnitude: Firms raise cloud computing productivity by 33% in their first year of adoption, taking up to 4 years to fully stabilize

design: Marketing Science Institute-commissioned synthesis of the empirical privacy-regulation literature
authors: Jean-Pierre Dubé, John G. Lynch, Dirk Bergemann, Mert Demirer, Avi Goldfarb, Garrett Johnson, Anja Lambrecht, Tesary Lin…
title: Frontiers: The Intended and Unintended Consequences of Privacy Regulation for Consumer Marketing
data: Synthesis of the empirical literature on GDPR, CCPA, and related privacy regulations' effects on advertising, competition, and consumer marketing
findings: The review concludes that privacy regulations like GDPR and CCPA generate real consumer privacy benefits but also impose unintended costs: they can reduce marketing effectiveness (particularly for personalized channels like display and email), raise compliance costs that fall disproportionately on small businesses and new entrants, and increase concentration among the largest data-holding incumbents, potentially entrenching dominant platforms' market power in digital advertising.
magnitude: Synthesizes evidence that privacy rules protect consumers but systematically raise concentration and burden small businesses more than large incumbents

design: Difference-in-differences on transatlantic (US-EU) venture capital investment flows
authors: Jian Jia, Ginger Zhe Jin, Mario Leccese, Liad Wagman
title: How Does Privacy Regulation Affect Transatlantic Venture Investment? Evidence from GDPR
period: Extends the Jia-Jin-Wagman (2021) sample with a longer post-…
data: Cross-border venture capital deal-level data tracking US investors funding EU startups (and vice versa) before and after GDPR
findings: Extending the analysis of short-run GDPR effects to focus specifically on transatlantic capital flows, the paper documents that GDPR is associated with a pullback specifically in cross-border (US-to-EU) venture investment, with distant US investors reducing funding to EU data-intensive startups more than domestic EU investors do, indicating GDPR raised the relative cost of information-intensive due diligence and monitoring for foreign investors.
magnitude: GDPR is associated with a disproportionate pullback in cross-border (US-to-EU) venture capital relative to domestic EU investment

design: Policy review of consumer-incentivized, e-invoice-based tax enforcement mechanisms
authors: Joana Naritomi, Tsogsag Nyamdavaa, Stephanie Campbell
title: Enlisting Consumers in Tax Enforcement: A Policy Review
data: Synthesis of programs using digital receipts and lottery/reward incentives to enlist consumers in monitoring firms' electronic sales reporting
findings: Reviews the design and effectiveness of consumer-facing digital tax-enforcement tools (e.g., receipt lotteries tied to e-invoicing) across countries, distilling design lessons on reward levels, fraud/collusion risks, and administrative complementarities needed for these programs to durably raise reported sales and revenue.
magnitude: Synthesizes cross-country evidence on when digital receipt-lottery schemes durably raise reported sales

design: Randomized controlled trial administering exam questions to law students with/without GPT-4
title: AI Assistance in Legal Analysis: An Empirical Study
data: RCT administering law school exam questions (multiple-choice and essay) to law students randomized to GPT-4 access or no AI access
findings: GPT-4 assistance significantly improved student performance on simple multiple-choice legal questions but did not significantly improve performance on complex essay questions requiring integrative legal reasoning, suggesting current-generation LLMs complement rather than replace higher-order legal analytical skills. This is among the first RCTs isolating AI's causal effect on human legal-reasoning tasks.
magnitude: Significant gains on multiple-choice legal questions; no significant gain on complex essay/legal-reasoning questions

design: Randomized and natural experiments around mandatory Aadhaar biometric authentication (ABBA) in the ration system
authors: Karthik Muralidharan, Paul Niehaus, Sandip Sukhtankar
title: Identity Verification Standards in Welfare Programs: Experimental Evidence from India
venue: Review of Economics and Statistics, 107(2), 372-392 (NBER WP 26744)
data: Large-scale randomized and natural-experiment variation in Aadhaar-based biometric authentication requirements in India's Public Distribution System (PDS)
findings: Requiring Aadhaar-based biometric authentication for the PDS reduced corruption/fraud in grain distribution but roughly 1.5-2 million eligible beneficiaries temporarily lost access to subsidized food at some point during the rollout. The adverse exclusion effects were driven primarily by how the technology transition was managed (e.g., abrupt cutovers, connectivity/seeding failures) rather than by biometrics per se.
magnitude: 1.5-2 million beneficiaries temporarily excluded despite reduced corruption

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Klaus Deininger et al. (2025) explore how digital technologies can improve the efficiency and inclusiveness of property registries. The study introduces a framework to assess digital registry services across three dimensions: digital coverage, interoperability, and the integration of property taxation for local service delivery and public land management. Analyzing data from 85 countries, the paper reveals significant disparities in digital registry adoption and performance. While some nations have made substantial progress in digitizing property records and enhancing interoperability between agencies, others lag due to infrastructural, legal, or institutional challenges. The authors advocate for strategic reforms that expand digital coverage and promote regular data collection to monitor progress. By strengthening property rights through digital registries, states can bolster public sector efficiency, support equitable economic growth, and foster a more livable environment.

design: Narrative review of economics and health-services literature on telehealth
authors: Kritee Gujral, S. Illarmo, Josephine C. Jacobs, Todd H. Wagner
title: The Economics of Telehealth: An Overview
region: Primarily United States (review also cites international literature)
data: Narrative review of medical and economics literature on telehealth demand, cost, utilization, and effectiveness
findings: Rigorous difference-in-differences studies mostly find telehealth modestly increases outpatient utilization rather than purely substituting for in-person care, with no significant impact on emergency or inpatient use in most studies reviewed. A meta-analysis of 76 RCTs found telehealth reduced all-cause hospitalization by 18 per 1,000 patients, and one study linked equalized cost-sharing between telehealth and in-person visits to a 6-9% reduction in mortality; the review stresses that rigorous economic evidence remains sparse outside the United States.
magnitude: Meta-analysis of 76 RCTs found telehealth cut all-cause hospitalization by 18 per 1,000 patients

design: Privacy-preserving classification of millions of real AI conversations mapped to O*NET occupational tasks
authors: Kunal Handa, Alex Tamkin, Miles McCain, Saffron Huang, Esin Durmus, Sarah Heck, Jared Mueller, Jerry Hong, Stuart Ritchi…
title: Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations
data: Over 4 million Claude.ai conversations classified by task and occupation via Anthropic's privacy-preserving Clio pipeline, mapped to the O*NET database
findings: Usage concentrates heavily in software development and writing tasks; about 36% of occupations use Claude for at least a quarter of their associated tasks, concentrated in mid-to-high-wage computer and mathematical occupations. Of classified task-level usage, 57% reflects augmentation (iterative collaboration, learning) while 43% reflects automation (directive requests with minimal human involvement).
magnitude: 57% of Claude usage is augmentation vs 43% automation; 36% of occupations use AI for ≥25% of their tasks

design: Task-level AI-exposure measures with instrumental-variables identification using historical university hiring networks
authors: Menaka Hampole, Dimitris Papanikolaou, Lawrence D.W. Schmidt, Bryan Seegmiller
title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market
data: Firm-occupation-level panel with NLP-derived measures of task exposure to AI/ML, 2010-2023, instrumented using historical university hiring networks
findings: Tasks with higher AI exposure subsequently see reduced labor demand, but the aggregate employment effect is modest because reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven employment increases elsewhere in adopting firms. Within firms, higher mean AI exposure depresses labor demand while greater exposure dispersion enables worker reallocation across tasks.
magnitude: AI exposure reduces demand in exposed tasks, but aggregate employment effects are modest due to offsetting productivity gains

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Evaluate the impact of integrating Aadhaar-based biometric authentication into India’s Public Distribution System (PDS), which provides subsidized food to over 800 million low-income individuals. Drawing on large-scale randomized controlled trials and administrative data, the study finds that biometric authentication reduced leakages by 11 percentage points - a 41% decline from baseline diversion levels - indicating improved public sector efficiency and targeting accuracy. However, this gain came with significant costs: authentication errors and poor transition management led to exclusion rates of 2–4%, translating to approximately 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries facing interruptions in access. These exclusions were largely driven by technological failures, such as connectivity issues and biometric mismatches. The authors emphasize that while digital ID systems can strengthen delivery by reducing fraud, careful attention to infrastructure readiness, user experience, and institutional safeguards is essential to avoid harming the very populations these systems are meant to serve.

design: Policy blueprint proposing a national AI compute capacity assessment framework
title: A Blueprint for Building National Compute Capacity for Artificial Intelligence
data: Policy analysis and expert consultation; no single quantitative dataset
findings: The report concludes that no country currently has sufficient data on, or a targeted plan for, its national AI compute capacity, calling this a policy 'blind spot' that could jeopardize economic goals. It proposes a three-dimensional framework -- capacity (availability/use of compute), effectiveness (people, policy, innovation, access), and resilience (security, sovereignty, sustainability) -- as the first structured blueprint for governments to plan around the global compute divide.
magnitude: OECD finds no country yet has adequate data or a plan for its own national AI compute capacity

design: Harmonized cross-country survey comparison (Global Survey of Working Arrangements)
authors: Pablo Zarate, Mathias Dolls, Steven J. Davis, Nicholas Bloom, Jose Maria Barrero, Cevat Giray Aksoy
title: Why Does Working From Home Vary Across Countries and People?
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
data: Harmonized cross-country Global Survey of Working Arrangements covering advanced and emerging economies
findings: Working-from-home rates vary widely across countries and are systematically related to national income, industry mix, commuting times, housing/dwelling characteristics, and broadband/digital-infrastructure quality, rather than to worker preferences alone; richer countries with better home internet and longer commutes show persistently higher WFH shares.
magnitude: Cross-country WFH gaps track digital infrastructure, income, and commute times more than worker preferences

design: Refined exposure index combining primary survey, expert Delphi review, and AI-based scoring
authors: Pawel Gmyrek, Janine Berg, Karol Kamiński, Filip Konopczyński, Agnieszka Ładna, Balint Nafradi, Konrad Rosłaniec, Marek…
title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure
data: 29,753 tasks rated by 1,640 employees across ISCO-08 occupational groups; 52,558 task-level automation-potential data points for 2,861 tasks; Delphi expert panels; AI-based scoring; four-tier exposure gradient
findings: Globally, one in four workers (25%) are in occupations with some generative AI exposure, though only 3.3% of global employment falls in the highest-exposure category. Exposure is highly unequal by income level (34% of employment exposed in high-income countries vs 11% in low-income countries) and by gender, with the gap widening as countries get richer: 9.6% of female employment vs 3.5% of male employment is in the highest-exposure category in high-income countries.
magnitude: High-income country exposure 34% vs low-income 11%; female highest-exposure share 9.6% vs male 3.5% in high-income countries

design: Randomized field experiment varying disclosure of AI-based job matching
authors: Sarah H. Bana, Kevin J. Boudreau
title: AI-Enabled Job Markets & Market Participation: A Field Experiment on How AI Shapes Jobseekers' Expectations of Competition
venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab Working Paper
countries: Online job-matching platform (country not specified in available summary)
data: Field experiment with 4,562 jobseekers on an online job-matching platform, randomized across AI-matching disclosure, human-matching, and control conditions
findings: Jobseeker participation was about one-quarter lower when AI-based matching was disclosed compared to a human-matching treatment or an undisclosed control condition. The effect was strongest among jobseekers with STEM backgrounds (greater AI familiarity) and appears driven by beliefs about match quality, what inputs AI uses, and the scale of competition faced, rather than simple AI aversion.
magnitude: ~25% lower jobseeker participation when AI-based matching was disclosed vs. human-matching/control

design: Nationally representative recurring survey measurement (Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes, SWAA)
authors: Shelby Buckman, Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom, Steven J. Davis
title: Measuring Work from Home
venue: NBER Working Paper (submitted to Journal of Human Resources)
data: Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes (SWAA), a large recurring US survey on remote-work patterns
findings: As of 2025, working from home accounts for about a quarter of all paid workdays among US workers aged 20-64, roughly 3.5 times its pre-pandemic (2019) level. WFH rates are about 7 percentage points higher for workers with children under age eight and about 2 points higher for women than men; desired WFH rates exceed actual rates in every major demographic group, especially women, parents of young children, and less-educated workers.
magnitude: US work-from-home has stabilized at ~25% of paid workdays, 3.5x the pre-pandemic level

design: Network/contagion simulation using Fedwire payment data (2022 JFE) extended with COVID-period stress test (2025 FRBNY)
authors: Thomas M. Eisenbach, Anna Kovner, Michael Junho Lee
title: When It Rains, It Pours: Cyber Vulnerability and Financial Conditions (building on "Cyber Risk and the U.S. Financial System: A Pre-Mortem Analysis," Journal of Financial Economics, 2022)
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Economic Policy Review, Vol. 31(1); companion paper in Journal of Financial Economics 145(3)
period: ~2 decades of payment data, with focus on 2020 (COVID-19 ons…
data: Simulation model of the Fedwire interbank payment network calibrated to daily payment flows; stress-tested using changes in payment activity/concentration during the COVID-19 shock
findings: A cyberattack that impairs payment operations at one or more large banks can propagate liquidity stress through the interbank payment network to otherwise healthy, unaffected banks, even without any solvency problems. During the onset of COVID-19 in 2020, increased concentration and intraday liquidity stress in payment activity raised the system's vulnerability to a cyber event by approximately 50% relative to the rest of 2020, showing that cyber vulnerability is state-dependent on financial conditions rather than constant.
magnitude: Payment-system vulnerability to a cyberattack rose by about 50% during the COVID-19 shock as liquidity conditions tightened

design: Instrumental variables using zipcode-level timing and speed of high-speed fiber broadband rollout to instrument for cloud adoption, UK firm panel
authors: Timothy DeStefano, Richard Kneller, Jonathan Timmis
title: Cloud Computing and Firm Growth
venue: Review of Economics and Statistics, Vol. 107(6)
data: UK firm-level administrative panel data combined with zipcode-level fiber broadband rollout timing and speed instruments
findings: Cloud adoption increases employment, revenue, and productivity growth for young firms, but their activity becomes concentrated in fewer establishments. For incumbent firms, cloud adoption produces smaller scale effects and weaker productivity gains, and instead drives restructuring through more establishment deaths and fewer births; both young and incumbent firms disperse their remaining establishments farther from headquarters after adopting cloud.
magnitude: Cloud computing raises employment and productivity growth for young firms while triggering establishment closures and geographic dispersion for incumbents

design: County-level logit entry model with Heckman two-stage selection correction on local demand, operating-cost, and fixed-cost shifters
title: Where the Cloud Rests: The Economic Geography of Data Centers
venue: Strategy Science (Harvard Business School Working Paper 21-042)
data: Census of 1,433 US data centers (1,386 third-party facilities scraped from Baxtel.com/Datacenters.com plus facilities of the 4 largest cloud providers) matched to county-level demand, cost, and tax-incentive variables
findings: Third-party data centers show a strong urban bias: 96.4% of counties hosting one are in Metropolitan Statistical Areas, and a one-standard-deviation increase in population density raises entry likelihood by 7.4 percentage points, while a similar increase in local information-sector employment share raises it by 1.9 points. Hyperscale cloud providers follow the opposite logic: only 73% of their host counties are in MSAs, and cloud entry is significantly more sensitive to input costs (higher industrial electricity prices discourage cloud-provider entry, odds ratio 0.40) than to local demand. Fixed costs of entry are about 24% higher in the most competitive (largest) markets.
magnitude: Third-party data centers cluster in cities (96.4% in MSAs) while hyperscale cloud data centers locate based on electricity costs, not local demand

design: Global policy report combining investment, compute, and governance-participation data
title: Technology and Innovation Report 2025: Inclusive Artificial Intelligence for Development
countries: Global, with emphasis on developing countries excluding China
data: Compiled data on global AI private investment, R&D spending concentration, and participation in AI governance forums across ~190 countries
