findings: Applies a difference-in-differences estimation using panel household survey data combined with geospatial information on the rollout of mobile broadband coverage in Tanzania. The results reveal that being covered by 3G networks has a large positive effect on total household consumption and poverty reduction, driven by positive impacts on labor-market outcomes. Being covered by 3G is associated with a 7 percent increase in consumption, 6 percent increase in food consumption, and 9 percent increase in non-food consumption. Basic need poverty rate declines by 5 percentage points. 3G coverage is positively associated with a 3 percentage points increase in labor-force participation. Working-age individuals living in areas covered by mobile internet witnessed an increase in labor-force participation, wage employment, and non-farm self-employment, and a decline in farm employment. These effects vary by age, gender, and skill level. Younger and more skilled men benefit the most through higher labor-force participation and wage employment, while high-skilled women benefit from transitions from self-employed farm work into non-farm employment.

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Compares how in-kind food assistance, and an electronic voucher-based program affect the delivery of aid in practice. The Government of Indonesia randomized across 105 districts the transition from in-kind rice to approximately equivalent electronic vouchers redeemable for rice and eggs at a network of private agents. Targeted households received 46 percent more assistance in voucher areas. For the bottom 15 percent of households at baseline, poverty fell 20 percent. Voucher recipients received higher-quality rice, and increased consumption of eggs. The results suggest moving from a manual in-kind to electronic voucher-based program reduced poverty through increased adherence to program design.

design: Randomized experiment, Staggered rollout
findings: Evaluated the impact of eBay's Seller Hub on small businesses through a field experiment conducted from May 12 to August 8, 2016. Seller Hub helps sellers track performance metrics, such as sales, traffic, and feedback, enabling quick responses to market changes and improved service quality. The randomized rollout to eBay sellers showed that Seller Hub access increased weekly sales by 3.6% on average, with adopters seeing a 12.5% increase. Benefits included higher quantities sold, better feedback scores, more new listings, and improved inventory management, all without significant changes in average prices. Sellers who actively used performance metrics saw greater benefits.

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Follow the introduction of mobile money for the first time in rural villages of Mozambique using a randomized field experiment. The paper finds that mobile money increased migration out of these villages, where lower agricultural activity and investment is observed. At the same time, remittances received and welfare of rural households increased, particularly when facing geo-referenced village-level floods and household-level idiosyncratic shocks. The paper suggests that mobile money can accelerate urbanization and structural change in Sub-Saharan Africa.

design: Instrumental variables — Bitcoin price movements instrument for local cryptomining electricity demand
title: When cryptomining comes to town: high electricity-use spillovers to the local economy
countries: United States (Upstate New York), with a comparative analysis for China
data: County electricity billing and load data, cryptomining facility locations, Bitcoin price series, local business and employment records
findings: Cryptomining's very large local electricity demand raises bills for everyone else on the same grid. Using Bitcoin price movements to instrument for mining activity, the paper finds that ratepayers in affected Upstate New York counties bore roughly $204 million in additional annual electricity costs for households and $92 million for small businesses. Increased local business tax revenue offset only part of this. In China, mining-related electricity rationing was associated with lower wages and reduced investment, indicating crowding out of other electricity users.
magnitude: $204 million extra annual household electricity costs and $92 million for small businesses in affected counties; tax gains offset only part of the burden

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Found that an initiative by the Afghan government to modernize its payroll system – requiring teachers to biometrically register and receive salary payments via mobile money – significantly reduced delays and improved educational outcomes and financial inclusion, but did not decrease payments to non-existent ghost workers.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Find that from 2018 to 2020, establishments with robots tend to be larger, with more employees and a higher share of production workers, while also exhibiting lower earnings per worker. The presence of robot integrators in a locality significantly increases the likelihood of that area being classified as a Robot Hub by 20-25 percentage points. The geographic concentration of robot adoption leads to localized spillover effects, impacting employment and productivity in those regions.

design: Instrumental variables
findings: Make use of the high-lightening area IV approach and focus specifically on Rwanda between 2002 (with no mobile internet coverage) and 2019. They find that “improvements in the coverage of 3G mobile internet technologies increase the share of employed individuals, among whom are both skilled and unskilled workers, with the former increasing at a faster rate, given their relatively small initial size; sectoral shift employment towards services and, within the service sector, to some high value-added and skill-intensive industries. A 10 percentage point increase in 3G coverage increases the share of working age population that is employed by 3.4 percentage points. Education, migration, and shifts in demand are instrumental in explaining these findings. A 10 percentage point increase in 3G coverage increases the average years of schooling by 0.15 years.

design: Instrumental variables
findings: Using an instrumental variable strategy that leverages the distance between municipalities and the nearest optical packet backbone node, Cambini et al. (2023) , covering data from 2013 to 2019, find that ultra-fast broadband access leads to a 2.9% increase in total factor productivity of the firm and a 3.9% increase in labor productivity. The benefits are most pronounced in the services sector. Additionally, firms with full-fiber connections experience higher productivity gains compared to those with mixed copper-fiber connections. The productivity gains from ultra-fast broadband access are largely driven by structural changes within firms, particularly a decrease in the share of low-skilled workers and an increase in the share of younger employees. This workforce reconfiguration facilitates a more efficient allocation of labor and better integration of digital technologies, thereby enhancing overall firm productivity.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Cambodia’s Financial Management Information System (FMIS) reform aimed to modernize core government financial operations, particularly improving timeliness and accuracy in reporting. The implementation helped streamline disbursements and supported the Ministry of Economy and Finance in making better fiscal decisions.

design: Textual analysis of 10-K/10-Q risk disclosures to build firm-level cyber-risk factor; asset-pricing tests
authors: Chris Florackis, Christodoulos Louca, Roni Michaely, Michael Weber
title: Cybersecurity Risk
venue: Review of Financial Studies, 36(1): 351-407 (NBER Working Paper 28196)
period: Not precisely specified in verified abstract; disclosure-era…
data: Computational textual analysis of cybersecurity risk disclosures in SEC 10-K/10-Q filings, validated against realized hacking incidents and human/LLM auditor coding
findings: The firm-level cybersecurity-risk exposure measure is higher in IT-intensive industries, correlates with the characteristics of firms that later suffer attacks, and predicts future cyberattacks. Portfolios of firms with high cyber-risk exposure outperform low-exposure portfolios by up to 8.3% per year on average, consistent with a priced risk premium, but these same high-exposure firms underperform during periods of elevated realized cybersecurity risk.
magnitude: High cyber-risk-exposure stock portfolios earn up to 8.3%/year excess return as compensation for priced cyber risk

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: The Dalberg study is based on qualitative analysis and case studies across six African countries. It examines the potential of digital jobs to create inclusive economic opportunities and assesses the digital economy's growth potential. Digital jobs are defined as positions that use information technology to deliver a product or service, encompassing both short-term and permanent roles in the formal sector. It highlights that digital skills can lead to higher wages and long-term job stability. It notes that digital jobs in the formal sector provide wages significantly higher than those in the informal sector. For example, youth wages in Ghana's IT Enabled Services program are 3.5 times higher than baseline wages and 5.5 times higher than the official minimum wages. Digital skills impact economic growth through mechanisms such as increased income, job stability, and enhanced employability. It emphasizes the role of ICT in facilitating access to information and services, supporting business growth, and creating new job opportunities.

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Analyze the impact of a 2021 reform in Ukraine that—after earlier digitization efforts did not produce desired results—mandated use of transparent online auctions by local governments rather than a central agency to lease rights to public agricultural land. The shift to a collusion-proof electronic auction system increased lease revenue by 175%. Had all public land that Ukraine transferred since 2015 been auctioned using post-reform mechanisms, local governments would receive incremental lease revenue of US$500 million per year for the duration of the lease. Where public land is important, reforms to ensure rights to such land are allocated transparently, competitively and in a decentralized way could improve social, economic, and environmental outcomes.

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Examines the effects of AI on realistic, complex, and knowledge-intensive tasks in collaboration with the Boston Consulting Group. For each one of a set of 18 realistic consulting tasks within the frontier of AI capabilities, consultants using AI were significantly more productive (they completed 12.2% more tasks on average, and completed tasks 25.1% more quickly), and produced significantly higher quality results (more than 40% higher quality compared to a control group). Consultants across the skills distribution benefited significantly from having AI augmentation, with those below the average performance threshold increasing by 43% and those above increasing by 17% compared to their own scores. For a task selected to be outside the frontier, however, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to produce correct solutions compared to those without AI.

design: Difference-in-differences, Staggered rollout
findings: Used a difference-in-differences approach to analyze the impact of fast internet on input markets in Turkey, leveraging the staggered expansion of optical fiber networks from 2012 to 2019. The study found that better internet connectivity led to significant improvements in firms' input sourcing strategies, with a 2% increase in real income in the median Turkish province and gains up to 27% in Istanbul. Firms reallocated their purchases towards suppliers with better internet connectivity and diversified their input sources by increasing the number of suppliers and reducing purchase concentration.

design: Instrumental variables
findings: Used an instrumental variables approach exploiting fiber broadband speeds to examine cloud computing's impact on firm growth from 2008 to 2015. Cloud adoption led to substantial improvements, particularly for young firms, with a 14.3% annual employment growth, a 15.9% annual sales increase, and a 42% reduction in IT investments per employee. Labor productivity also increased significantly. Cloud computing resulted in 4 percentage points more jobs for the UK and dispersed employment farther from headquarters (21.71 km). Cloud enables young firms to scale quickly, while incumbents see weaker productivity gains and restructure with establishment deaths and fewer births due to reduced fixed IT costs and increased operational flexibility.

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Use transactions-level data on credit and debit cards from Visa, Inc. between 2007 and 2017 to quantify the resulting consumer surplus. The paper estimates e-commerce reached 8 percent of consumption by 2017, yielding the equivalent of a 1 percent boost to their consumption, or over $1,000 per household per year. While some of the gains arose from avoiding travel costs to local merchants, most of the gains stemmed from substituting to merchants available online but not locally. Higher income consumers gained more, as did consumers in more densely populated counties.

design: Difference-in-differences (staggered 3G rollout x municipal-election panel)
title: Mobile Internet access and political outcomes: Evidence from South Africa
data: GSMA granular (1km x 1km) mobile internet coverage data combined with South African municipal electoral panel data
findings: Mobile internet arrival raises voter turnout by about 2 percentage points and cuts the ruling party's vote share by about 3 percentage points, while increasing both the effective number of parties and the incidence of protests. Effects are consistent with both an information channel (revealing corruption/service-delivery failures) and a coordination channel facilitating collective action.
magnitude: +2pp voter turnout; -3pp ruling-party vote share following 3G arrival in South African municipalities

design: Lab-in-the-field / online experiment on scam-message identification
authors: Elif Kubilay, Eva Raiber, Lisa Spantig, Jana Cahlíková, Lucy Kaaria
title: Financial Fraud in Developing Countries: Common Scam Detection Tips Do Not Help Distinguish Scam From Non-Scam Messages
venue: ECONtribute Policy Brief No. 056 / CEPR VoxEU
data: Online experiment in Kenya (registered as an AEA RCT, ID AEARCTR-0008754) presenting participants with a mix of real scam and legitimate financial/mobile-money messages, with randomized provision of standard scam-detection guidance
findings: Conventional scam-detection tips (e.g., 'watch for spelling errors,' 'be wary of urgency') do not improve participants' ability to distinguish fraudulent from legitimate financial messages. Providing these tips instead makes people over-cautious, increasing false positives, partly because genuine official communications often contain the same 'red flag' features the tips warn about, undermining trust in legitimate mobile money and financial-service communications.
magnitude: Standard scam-detection tips fail to raise scam-identification accuracy and instead increase false-positive suspicion of legitimate financial messages

design: Field experiment with firms on an online job portal, randomizing paid advertising and applicant identity verification
title: Hiring Frictions and the Promise of Online Job Portals: Evidence from India
data: Field experiment with firms using an online job portal, randomizing access to paid advertising and applicant identity verification
findings: Run a field experiment with firms recruiting through an online job portal in India, randomizing access to paid job advertising and to a feature that verifies applicants’ identity and credentials. Both frictions bind: firms offered paid advertising together with applicant identity verification increased hiring by 68 percent relative to control, showing that information frictions — not merely a shortage of applicants — hold back formal-sector hiring on digital job platforms.
magnitude: Advertising plus identity verification on a job portal raised firm hiring by 68%

design: Difference-in-differences on web-technology vendor counts and market concentration
authors: Garrett A. Johnson, Scott K. Shriver, Samuel G. Goldberg
title: Privacy and Market Concentration: Intended and Unintended Consequences of the GDPR
data: Website-level counts of web technology vendors (analytics, ad-tech) before and after GDPR, comparable to related comScore/vendor-tracking panels used in this literature
findings: GDPR increased concentration among web technology vendors, an unintended consequence working against the regulation's competition goals: the number of vendors serving the average website fell, and market share shifted toward the largest incumbent providers, which had more resources to adapt to compliance costs. The paper frames this as a case where privacy regulation's compliance-cost burden falls disproportionately on smaller ad-tech vendors, harming short-run competition even as it advances privacy protection.
magnitude: GDPR increased web-technology vendor market concentration, with the largest incumbents gaining relative share as smaller vendors exited

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Between 2017 and 2022, Google’s data center investments in Loudoun County generated an average of ~$800 million per year in direct, ~$180 million in indirect, and ~$100 million in induced economic impacts, as measured by GDP — ~$1.1 billion on average, in total, per year and ~$2.0 billion in total in the most recent year of study, 2022. (Source: Google and Deloitte Report, 2023)

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Gunsilius and Van Dijcke (2023) uses a non-parametric regression method to show that an internet shutdown in India resulted in a reduction of economic activity by 25--35%, greatly surpassing previous estimates and shedding new light on the true cost of such shutdowns for digital economies globally.

design: Structural model of consumer opt-out and advertiser valuation using proprietary ad-tech tracking/prediction data
authors: Guy Aridor, Yeon-Koo Che, Tobias Salz
title: The Effect of Privacy Regulation on the Data Industry: Empirical Evidence from GDPR
venue: RAND Journal of Economics, 54(4) (NBER Working Paper 26900)
data: Anonymized data from a third-party advertising intermediary tracking keyword searches and purchases for online travel agencies, including the intermediary's proprietary consumer-prediction algorithm
findings: GDPR's opt-in consent requirement caused a 12.5% drop in the number of consumers the intermediary could observe/track. However, privacy-conscious consumers who opt out exert a positive information externality on those who remain opted in, making the remaining pool more predictable; the intermediary's ability to predict consumer behavior did not significantly worsen, and the average value of remaining tracked consumers to advertisers rose, partially offsetting the losses from reduced tracking coverage.
magnitude: GDPR's opt-in rule cut the tracked consumer pool by 12.5%, but the value of each remaining tracked consumer rose, partly offsetting advertiser losses

design: Descriptive policy analysis and cross-country comparison of instant payment system design
title: Pix: Brazil's Successful Instant Payment System
venue: IMF Country Report No. 23/289 (Brazil: Selected Issues)
data: Descriptive/comparative analysis of the design and rollout of Pix, Brazil's central-bank-run instant payment system, benchmarked against instant payment systems in other countries
findings: The paper attributes Pix's rapid, large-scale adoption to design choices such as free peer-to-peer transfers, central-bank operation, simple QR-code/alias-based use, and mandatory participation by large banks, contrasting this with the slower adoption of instant payment systems elsewhere that left more design choices to private banks.
magnitude: Identifies central-bank-mandated, zero-fee design as the key driver of Pix's unusually fast mass adoption

design: Event study of equity/commodity markets around a critical-infrastructure ransomware attack
title: Commodity Market Interactions With Energy-Firm Distress: Evidence From the Colonial Pipeline Ransomware Attack
period: May 2021 (Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack and surroundin…
data: High-frequency equity and commodity (energy futures) price data surrounding the six-day Colonial Pipeline shutdown following the DarkSide ransomware attack
findings: The ransomware-induced shutdown of Colonial Pipeline generated measurable distress spillovers from the energy firm into related commodity markets, with energy futures and related equities showing significant co-movement and volatility around the attack window, illustrating how a ransomware attack on a single pipeline operator propagated into broader financial and commodity market pricing.
magnitude: Ransomware shutdown of a single pipeline operator produced significant, measurable spillovers into energy commodity markets during the 6-day outage

design: difference-in-differences exploiting geographic variation in mobile-broadband coverage expansion
authors: Kalvin Bahia, Pau Castells, Genaro Cruz, Takaaki Masaki, Carlos Rodriguez-Castelan, Viviane Sanfelice
title: Mobile Broadband Internet, Poverty and Labor Outcomes in Tanzania
data: Geo-coded 3G/4G network coverage maps merged with household panel survey data
findings: Expanding mobile broadband coverage is associated with reduced household poverty and improved labor-market outcomes, with effects concentrated in non-farm wage employment and business activity; the paper highlights that rural areas lagging in broadband coverage also lag in these poverty-reduction gains, underscoring the rural-urban digital divide's economic stakes.
magnitude: Mobile broadband expansion is linked to reduced poverty and improved labor outcomes, concentrated in non-farm activity

design: General-equilibrium analysis of the same randomized Smartcard payments-infrastructure rollout, using local labor-market data
authors: Karthik Muralidharan, Paul Niehaus, Sandip Sukhtankar
title: General Equilibrium Effects of (Improving) Public Employment Programs: Experimental Evidence from India
data: Same Smartcard RCT infrastructure as Muralidharan et al. (2016), linked to household earnings/wage and local labor-market survey data
findings: Improving delivery of India's NREGS employment guarantee via biometric payments infrastructure raised beneficiary household earnings by 14% and reduced poverty by 26%. Strikingly, 86% of the income gains came from non-program earnings, driven by higher private-sector wages and employment as the improved public program tightened local labor markets and raised reservation wages.
magnitude: 86% of poverty-reducing income gains came from spillovers to private-sector wages, not the transfer itself

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Investigate how the discretion of bureaucrats involved in the expansion of the tax roll affects its accuracy and equity. In the first digital property tax census in Dakar, Senegal, the authors randomly assign neighborhoods to valuation methods with different degrees of bureaucrat discretion. Compared to a benchmark of market values provided by licensed real estate assessors, bureaucrats in full discretion areas undervalue properties. This undervaluation is more severe for higher-value properties, resulting in a regressive tax profile: the median tax rate is 3.8% in the lowest quintile and 1.7% in the top quintile, instead of the expected 4.4% and 8.6% rates based on the tax code. A rule-based system in which an algorithm incorporates bureaucrat inputs to predict property values significantly reduces this tax gap, but a pure rule system with no bureaucrat input yields the highest accuracy and equity. Using a lab-in-the-field experiment, we identify bureaucrats’ lack of knowledge about high-end properties and fairness concerns as key mechanisms. In contrast, we find no evidence of collusion between bureaucrats and property owners.

design: Theoretical endogenous growth model with full automation of production and R&D
title: Economic Growth under Transformative AI
data: No empirical data; growth-theoretic model exploring automation of production and of R&D itself
findings: If AI can fully automate production (including self-replicating capital), the model implies growth rates could rise dramatically while labor's income share falls sharply, breaking historically stable 'Kaldor facts' about constant factor shares. Automating R&D alone can accelerate this transition further but the paper shows it may not be sufficient by itself; whether wages rise or fall depends on returns to scale, resource constraints, and the direction of technical change. The paper offers a qualitative theoretical framework rather than point-estimate growth forecasts.
magnitude: Theoretical result: full automation could break the long-stable Kaldor facts, sharply raising growth while cutting labor's income share

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Used a difference-in-differences approach to analyze internet adoption in over 150 countries from 1997 to 2021. Internet use increased secondary school test scores by 16% and labor force participation by 6-10 percentage points, especially benefiting women. Higher internet use in lower-income countries led to greater labor force participation. Reductions in unpaid work for women were noted, due to enhanced access to information and services.

design: Staggered rollout, Panel regression
findings: Investigate the impacts of school-based internet access on second graders' test scores, using over 2 million student observations from a panel of Peruvian public primary schools. The paper identifies effects up to 6+ years after installation on different cohorts of second-grade students, exploiting variation in the timing of internet access induced by the rollout of a national program. It finds positive but modest short-run impacts, but importantly, these effects grow for subsequent cohorts. Indeed, short-run estimates alone would have led to different conclusions. These dynamics underscore the value of extended evaluation windows to allow benefits of educational technology to materialize.

design: Machine-learning weather model benchmarked against operational numerical weather prediction
authors: Lam, R., Sanchez-Gonzalez, A. et al. (Google DeepMind)
title: Learning Skillful Medium-Range Global Weather Forecasting (GraphCast)
period: Trained on ERA5 reanalysis data; evaluated 2018-2022
data: Graph neural network trained on historical (ERA5) atmospheric reanalysis data, benchmarked against the ECMWF's operational HRES forecasting system across 1,380 verification targets and 227 weather variables at 0.25-degree resolution
findings: GraphCast significantly outperformed the leading operational forecasting system (ECMWF HRES) on 90% of 1,380 verification targets for 10-day global forecasts, while generating a full forecast in under one minute on standard hardware versus hours on a supercomputer for physics-based models. This is a leading example of AI-for-climate application -- cheaper, faster, more accurate weather forecasting -- which is central to climate adaptation and disaster early-warning in resource-constrained countries.
magnitude: GraphCast beat the leading operational weather model on 90% of forecast targets while running in under a minute versus hours

design: difference-in-differences comparing media markets differentially exposed to a given cable news program
authors: Leonardo Bursztyn, Aakaash Rao, Christopher P. Roth, David H. Yanagizawa-Drott
title: Opinions as Facts
venue: Review of Economic Studies (earlier circulated as NBER Working Paper 27417, "Misinformation During a Pandemic")
data: Media-market-level exposure to two popular cable news shows with divergent early COVID-19 coverage, matched to health/behavioral outcomes
findings: Media-market areas with greater exposure to a cable news host who downplayed COVID-19's severity in February-March 2020 subsequently exhibited less social distancing and, ultimately, higher COVID-19 case growth and mortality relative to areas with more exposure to a host on the same network who treated the virus as a serious threat, showing that differential misinformation exposure from an otherwise similar outlet had measurable public-health consequences.
magnitude: Greater exposure to COVID-19-downplaying cable news coverage was followed by less social distancing and higher subsequent case/death growth

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Evaluate the extent to which small businesses maintain an online presence, looking at restaurant listings on a major online review platform. While the majority of restaurants have an online presence, the paper finds that roughly 18 percent in the sample have no presence as of the end of 2017, despite being able to list their business for free. Using temporal variation in a restaurant's online presence as well as a natural experiment arising from a data acquisition that led over a thousand businesses to be added to the platform, the paper finds that maintaining an online presence is valuable for small businesses. Establishing an online presence leads to a 5% revenue increase. Using data on customer reviews post-add, the paper explores potential channels that could explain why restaurants continue to remain offline despite potential benefits from digital representation. Consistent with models of voluntary disclosure, it finds that businesses that had stayed offline until the acquisition ended up having lower ratings, on average, than those that added themselves or were added by customers.

design: Life-cycle carbon accounting of a large language model's training compute
title: Estimating the Carbon Footprint of BLOOM, a 176B Parameter Language Model
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research, Vol. 24
data: Direct measurement and life-cycle estimation of energy use and embodied emissions (hardware manufacturing plus operation) for training the 176-billion-parameter BLOOM model
findings: BLOOM's final training run emitted approximately 24.7 tonnes of CO2-equivalent, substantially lower than several comparable large language models when accounting for the low-carbon electricity grid used, though the paper stresses that estimates vary widely depending on whether embodied hardware emissions and inference-phase emissions (which can exceed training emissions over a model's lifetime) are included.
magnitude: Training BLOOM (176B parameters) emitted an estimated 24.7 tonnes of CO2-equivalent, illustrating how grid carbon-intensity drives LLM footprints

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Examined data center employment dynamics using interviews and observations. They found a tension between job creation and destruction due to predicted 40% automation in the next three years, leading to anxieties about labor shortages and a global vacancy of 100,000 jobs. "Stand-by" labor creates feelings of both job security and redundancy, with workers experiencing boredom and stress. Despite diversification efforts, significant gender and racial disparities persist.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Use data analysis to assess the digitalization (Level and importance of digital content in occupations. High digitalization jobs require robust knowledge of computers and electronics) of work across various U.S. occupations, states, and metro areas. It employs digitalization scores derived from the O*NET survey to measure the digital content of jobs. Digitalization has significantly increased across the U.S. workforce, with more than 26% of jobs now requiring high levels of digital skills. Wage premiums associated with high digitalization jobs are rising, with average earnings being $79,000 compared to $54,000 for medium-level and $35,000 for low-level digitalization jobs. Mechanisms such as increased productivity, higher wages, and the facilitation of remote work as pathways through which digital skills impact economic growth. It emphasizes the role of digital skills in enabling workers to adapt to technological changes and access better job opportunities.

design: Descriptive analysis of a global census of online gig-work platforms and job-posting data
title: Working Without Borders: The Promise and Peril of Online Gig Work
data: Census of 545 online gig-work platforms and associated job-posting/traffic data, 2016-2023
findings: Online gig work is estimated at up to 12% of the global labor market, with 40% of platform traffic originating in low- and middle-income countries. Job postings on these platforms grew 130% in Sub-Saharan Africa versus 14% in North America, and almost 60% of firms in poorer countries increased their use of gig outsourcing versus under 50% in wealthier countries. Women are overrepresented on gig platforms relative to local labor markets but earn only 68% of what men earn on major platforms.
magnitude: Sub-Saharan Africa gig job postings grew 130% vs 14% in North America; women earn 68% of men's platform wages

design: Cross-sectional association
findings: National Governors Association (2022) qualitatively analyses and conducts case studies of digital skills initiatives across six U.S. states. It reviews the strategies these states are employing to advance digital skills among their workforces. Digital skills include basic digital literacy and advanced competencies related to specific technologies and digital tools. The report discusses mechanisms such as increased employability, enhanced productivity, and improved access to higher-paying jobs as pathways through which digital skills contribute to economic growth. For instance, in Oklahoma, each additional point added to a worker’s “digital skills score,” on a scale of 0-100, is associated with an extra $781 in annual earnings; increasing a North Dakotan’s “digital skills score” by one point on a scale of 0-100 can increase annual income by an average of just under $660. These earnings will indirectly impact economic growth due to increased spending.

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Summarized the impact of generative AI on employee productivity using data from three distinct studies. Customer service agents using AI handled 13.8% more inquiries per hour. Business professionals writing documents with AI saw a 59% increase in productivity. Programmers using AI completed 126% more coding tasks per week. The average productivity gain across all studies was 66%, with the greatest benefits observed in more complex tasks and among less-skilled workers.

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Investigated the impact of ChatGPT on productivity in professional writing tasks using a pre-registered online experiment with 444 participants. The study utilized a difference-in-differences methodology. Results show ChatGPT decreased task completion time by 37% and increased quality by 0.45 standard deviations, especially benefiting lower-ability workers.

design: Institutional synthesis of employer/worker surveys and occupational exposure measures
title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market (OECD Employment Outlook 2023, Chapter 4)
data: OECD employer and worker surveys on AI use combined with occupational AI-exposure measures
findings: Employment in occupations most exposed to AI continued to grow rather than shrink through 2023, with no detectable AI-driven decline in labor demand yet. AI is distinctive relative to earlier automation because it can perform non-routine cognitive tasks (reasoning, language, perception), so effects are more likely to appear first as changes in tasks and job quality than as outright job loss; wages should rise for workers whose skills complement AI but could fall for those squeezed into a shrinking task set.
magnitude: No detectable AI-driven employment decline yet in the most AI-exposed OECD occupations as of 2023

design: Review synthesizing case studies and interviews with African tax administrators on IT-enabled tax administration
title: Increasing Tax Collection in African Countries: The Role of Information Technology
data: Case studies and interviews with senior African tax officials on IT tools for consumption, property, trade, and income tax administration
findings: As of 2018, Sub-Saharan African countries collected on average 14% of GDP in taxes, with high-capacity countries (Seychelles, Namibia, South Africa) reaching 28-33% versus about 7% in low-capacity states (Chad, DRC). The review finds IT tools (e-filing, electronic sales registers, digitized property cadastres) can help close this gap by improving identification of the tax base and detection of evasion, but their effectiveness depends heavily on complementary administrative capacity.
magnitude: Sub-Saharan Africa's average tax-to-GDP ratio (14%) masks a 7%-33% range tied partly to IT-enabled administration capacity

design: Event study around CCPA passage (2018) and enforcement (2020) using retail-sector stock returns
authors: Pankaj C. Patel, Pejvak Oghazi, S. Arunachalam
title: Does Consumer Privacy Act Influence Firm Performance in the Retail Industry? Evidence from a US State-Level Law Change
data: Stock market event-study data for a sample of US retail firms around CCPA's passage and enforcement dates
findings: CCPA's passage did not produce a statistically meaningful average stock market reaction across the full sample of retail firms, but firms with greater intangible-asset intensity, and firms with both higher complexity and intangibility, realized significantly positive cumulative abnormal returns, suggesting investors expected some retailers (particularly those with strong existing data/brand assets) to benefit competitively from the new privacy regime relative to peers.
magnitude: CCPA had no average stock-market effect on retailers, but firms with high intangible-asset intensity saw significantly positive abnormal returns

design: Industry-commissioned economic-impact estimation (before/after comparison plus macro impact modeling), not a peer-reviewed causal study
title: Economic Impact of 2Africa (and related country studies: DRC, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania)
countries: DRC, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania; 33 countries along the 2Africa cable route
data: National accounts/employment data before and after submarine-cable landings, combined with macroeconomic impact modeling for the projected effects of the new 2Africa cable
findings: In the DRC, the 2012 subsea-cable landing is associated with an 8.2% increase in employment in fiber-connected areas and a 19% increase in national GDP per capita. The 2Africa cable (activating 2023/24, circumnavigating Africa with 46 landing stations across 33 countries) is projected to add $26.2-36.9 billion to African economies within 2-3 years of activation, equivalent to roughly 0.4-0.6% of Africa's PPP GDP.
magnitude: DRC: +8.2% employment / +19% GDP per capita post-cable-landing; 2Africa projected at +$26-37bn (~0.5% of Africa's PPP GDP) within 2-3 years

design: Preregistered online RCT with incentivized occupation-specific writing tasks
title: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence
data: 453 college-educated professionals randomly assigned ChatGPT access (or not) for incentivized, occupation-specific writing tasks
findings: ChatGPT access cut average task completion time by 40% and raised output quality (graded by peers) by 18%. Gains were concentrated among lower-ability workers, compressing the productivity distribution across participants. The tool shifted task composition toward idea generation and editing and away from rough drafting, and increased both job satisfaction/self-efficacy and concern about automation.
magnitude: 40% reduction in task completion time; 18% increase in output quality

design: Structural demand estimation (random-coefficients nested logit + Bertrand-Nash supply, BLP-style) on handset-model-level sales data
title: Adoption of Digital Technologies: The Case of Smartphones in India
venue: Working paper (Toulouse School of Economics; presented at ISI Delhi ACEGD 2023)
data: IDC handset-model-level sales and price data (9,534 models, 27,730 model-quarter observations), World Inequality Database income percentiles, and GSMA 3G/4G coverage data
findings: Estimates a structural demand-and-supply model of the smartphone market: the own-price elasticity of smartphone demand is -11.1, and consumers in the bottom 60% of the income distribution are about 4 times more price-sensitive than the top 40%. Counterfactual simulations show the market would be 35% smaller absent the observed device-quality improvements, 20% smaller absent income growth, and 12% smaller absent 3G/4G network rollout. India's 2020 GST hike on phones (12% to 18%) is estimated to have cut smartphone sales by 5.7%, while a targeted $10 subsidy for low-income buyers achieves comparable adoption gains far more cheaply than flat subsidies or tax cuts.
magnitude: Smartphone demand elasticity of -11.1; 2020 GST hike (12%->18%) cut sales by 5.7%; a targeted $10 subsidy reaches the same adoption gain at ~13% of the government revenue cost of a flat tax cut (vs. 30-43%)

design: Randomized controlled trial comparing developers with vs. without Copilot
authors: Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer
title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
data: RCT assigning recruited software developers an HTTP server implementation task in JavaScript, with or without GitHub Copilot access
findings: Studied the impact of GitHub Copilot on developer productivity through a controlled experiment involving 95 programmers recruited via Upwork. The experiment, conducted between May 15 and June 20, 2022, tasked participants with implementing an HTTP server in JavaScript. The treatment group, using GitHub Copilot, completed the task 55.8% faster than the control group, showing a significant increase in productivity. Developers with less experience, those who code more hours per day, and older programmers benefitted the most from using Copilot.
magnitude: 55.8% faster task completion with Copilot access

design: Diff-in-differences exploiting geographic variation in demonetization-induced cash-shortage intensity
authors: Sutirtha Das, Lucie Gadenne, Tushar Nandi, Ross Warwick
title: Does Going Cashless Make You Tax-Rich? Evidence from India's Demonetization Experiment
data: Firm-level corporate tax return data linked to local intensity of the 2016 demonetization cash shock
findings: Areas more exposed to India's 2016 demonetization shock saw faster growth in electronic payments and larger increases in firm sales reported to the tax authority. The rise in electronic payments is estimated to explain roughly half of the 11% aggregate increase in reported sales observed during demonetization, indicating that digital payments strengthen tax authorities' ability to observe firms' true tax base.
magnitude: Electronic-payment growth explains about half of the 11% rise in reported firm sales after demonetization

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Ta and Turner Lee (2023) analyzed the constraints that language gaps impose on the development of generative AI. They observed that generative AI tools, predominantly trained on English and a few other data-rich languages, fail to adequately represent over 7,000 languages spoken worldwide. This linguistic bias exacerbates social and economic divisions, with English and other high-resource languages dominating AI training data.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Research shows that technology has the potential to contribute up to $15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030, of which $1.2 trillion could be generated in Africa, representing a 5.6 percent increase in the continent’s GDP by 2030. (Source: UN Africa Renewal)

design: agency global status report based on national self-assessments
authors: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) and World Meteorological Organization (WMO)
title: Global Status of Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems 2023
countries: Global, with regional breakdowns (highest disaster exposure in Asia-Pacific)
data: National multi-hazard early warning system (MHEWS) coverage self-assessments compiled under the Sendai Framework monitoring system
findings: Countries with less comprehensive multi-hazard early warning systems have a disaster-related mortality ratio nearly six times higher than countries with substantial-to-comprehensive systems. The report documents mobile technologies (cell broadcast, SMS) as an increasingly central channel for last-mile warning dissemination, particularly in Asia-Pacific, which accounts for about 75% of people affected by disasters worldwide, underpinning the UN 'Early Warnings for All' initiative targeting universal coverage by 2027.
magnitude: Countries with weak multi-hazard early warning systems have ~6x higher disaster mortality than those with strong systems

design: Descriptive cross-country data report
title: Digital Progress and Trends Report 2023
data: Cross-country data on firm digital-technology investment, internet use/affordability/quality, digital-services trade, and IT-sector value added
findings: Firms' digital-technology investment surged from 13% to 54% in East Asia between 2020 and 2022, while adoption remained below 30% by end-2022 in most other developing regions; investment roughly doubled among micro firms (10% to 20%) and tripled among large firms (20% to 60%). The digital sector remains highly concentrated: the top six economies account for 70% of global IT-services value added, even though the sector grows about twice as fast as the overall economy and creates jobs at roughly six times the global average rate.
magnitude: East Asia firm digital investment: 13% to 54% (2020-22) vs. under 30% in most other developing regions; top-6 economies hold 70% of global IT-services value-added

design: Difference-in-differences / event study around ChatGPT's release using platform microdata
authors: Xiang Hui, Oren Reshef, Luofeng Zhou
title: The Short-Term Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Employment: Evidence from an Online Labor Market
data: Job- and freelancer-level data from the Upwork online labor marketplace before/after ChatGPT's release, focused on writing- and coding-related gigs
findings: Following ChatGPT's release, automation-exposed freelance job categories on Upwork saw about a 2% drop in the number of jobs posted and a 5.2% drop in freelancers' monthly earnings, concentrated in writing- and coding-related gigs most substitutable by generative AI. This provides some of the first platform-level causal evidence of generative AI displacing online gig/freelance work.
magnitude: ChatGPT's release associated with -2% jobs and -5.2% monthly earnings for exposed Upwork freelancers

design: large-scale behavioral telemetry combined with lifecycle/household carbon-footprint modeling
authors: Yanqiu Tao, Longqi Yang, Sonia Jaffe, Fereshteh Amini, Peter Bergen, Brent Hecht, Fengqi You
title: Climate mitigation potentials of teleworking are sensitive to changes in lifestyle and workplace rather than ICT usage
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
data: Large-scale workplace telemetry/survey data combined with lifecycle carbon-footprint modeling of commuting, office energy, and home-office energy use
findings: Full-time telework can reduce an individual's work-related carbon footprint by up to 58% in the US, but the size of the effect depends far more on lifestyle changes (vehicle ownership, non-commute travel, home-office energy use) than on the ICT devices used for telework itself. Partial telework of one day per week at home cuts emissions by only about 2%, while working from home two to four days per week cuts emissions by 11%-29%; benefits can be partly offset by increased household vehicle ownership and home energy use.
magnitude: Full-time telework can cut a worker's carbon footprint up to 58%, but only ~2% for one remote day per week

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Examined the impact of AI on translators using Google's neural network-based translation (GNNT) over the period from January 2016 to May 2017. Employing a difference-in-differences design, they found a significant reduction in human translation tasks, particularly those requiring analytical skills, with a 13-20% drop in regular translation tasks. Conversely, tasks requiring cultural and emotional intelligence were less affected. Translator earnings decreased by $352,000 in the six months following GNNT’s introduction, without evidence of price adjustments.

design: Machine-learning targeting model trained on satellite and mobile-phone metadata, validated against household survey ground truth
authors: Emily Aiken, Suzanne Bellue, Joshua E. Blumenstock, Dean Karlan, Christopher Udry
title: Machine Learning and Phone Data Can Improve Targeting of Humanitarian Aid
data: Mobile network operator call-detail records, satellite imagery, and household survey data used to target Togo's COVID-19 Novissi emergency cash-transfer program
findings: Using machine-learning models trained on mobile-phone metadata and satellite imagery to identify the poorest mobile subscribers, Togo's government digitally targeted emergency cash transfers to roughly 140,000 additional people in the country's poorest cantons within weeks of program design, entirely remotely, without door-to-door enumeration.
magnitude: ML+phone-data targeting delivered COVID cash aid to ~140,000 additional poor residents within weeks

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Examine how the adoption of information communication technology affects bilateral trade. The context is a public program in Norway that rolled out broadband access points leading to plausibly exogenous variation in the availability and adoption of broadband by firms. It finds that broadband makes trade patterns more sensitive to distance and economic size. These results are consistent with a model of trade with variable elasticity of demand. The model predicts that adoption of a technology that lowers information frictions enlarges the choice set of exporters and importers. This makes demand more elastic with respect to trade costs and thus distance.

design: nationally representative demand-side household survey
authors: Asli Demirguc-Kunt, Leora Klapper, Dorothe Singer, Saniya Ansar
title: The Global Findex Database 2021: Financial Inclusion, Digital Payments, and Resilience in the Age of COVID-19
data: Gallup World Poll-based Global Findex household survey on financial account ownership and digital payments
findings: Account ownership in developing economies rose from 63% to 71% between 2017 and 2021, while the gender gap in account ownership across developing economies narrowed from 9 to 6 percentage points. Globally, the gender gap in account ownership fell to 4 percentage points for the first time on record (78% of men banked vs. 74% of women), a narrowing driven substantially by growth in mobile-money and other digital-payment accounts.
magnitude: Global gender gap in financial account ownership fell to 4 percentage points in 2021

design: Staggered rollout
findings: Examine the effect of computer-assisted learning on students’ long-term development. It explores the implementation of a large ed-tech intervention that connected some of China’s best teachers to more than 100 million rural students through satellite internet. By leveraging the staggered installation of computer equipment in different areas of the country, the paper finds evidence that exposure to the program improved students’ academic achievement, labor performance, and computer usage. Treated counties increased years of education by 0.75 years. Relative to individuals who were 15 at the time of the policy, for example, completed education increased by 0.89 years among 14-year-olds, by 0.90 years among 13-year-olds, by 0.79 years among 12-year-olds, by 1.31 years among 11-year-olds, and by 1.30 years among 10-year-olds. They estimate a remarkable reduction in urban-rural education and earnings gaps of 21 and 78%, respectivel. These effects are observed up to ten years after program implementation. These findings indicate that education technology can have long-lasting positive effects on a variety of outcomes and can be effective in reducing the rural–urban education gap.

design: Difference-in-differences, Panel regression
findings: Blind, Niebel, and Rammer (2022) provides empirical evidence on the impact of the GDPR on innovation activities in firms. Exploiting panel data from the German innovation survey, a difference-in-difference analysis shows that the GDPR stimulated additional innovation activity while shifting the focus of innovation away from radical and towards more incremental innovation. GDPR increased the sales share of new-to-firm innovations by 0.9-3.3 percentage points, while reduces the sales share of new-to-market innovations by 0.6-1.5 percentage points. This holds for both firms that report that the GDPR complicated their innovation efforts, and for the much smaller group of firms that report that the GDPR facilitated their innovation activities. Finally, larger and older firms experience higher increases in their turnover with incremental innovation compared to smaller and younger firms.

design: Panel regressions using timing of 3G rollout across 6,802 sub-national regions
title: The Employment Effects of Mobile Internet in Developing Countries
data: IPUMS International census/survey microdata for 6,802 sub-national regions (16,069 region-year observations) matched to 3G network rollout timing
findings: 3G expansion significantly raises female labor force participation and employment rates for both men and women. Men shift out of unpaid agricultural/service work into small owner-operated enterprises and service-sector wage jobs, while women take up unpaid agricultural jobs vacated by men and start small non-farm enterprises. The pattern resembles expansion of informal 'gig-economy' activity rather than structural transformation into manufacturing.
magnitude: 3G rollout raises employment rates for both sexes and female labor force participation across 14 LMICs (2000-2015), operating mainly through informal self-employment rather than formal job creation

design: Instrumental variables
findings: Examine the employment impacts of mobile internet expansion from 2G to 3G networks across 14 low- and middle-income countries. Employing an instrumental variable strategy based on the slower 3G expansion in high-lightening areas, they find that a 10 percentage point increase in 3G coverage increases employment rates by 2.1 percentage points.

design: Difference-in-differences tracking third-party web-technology vendors on a large website panel pre/post GDPR
authors: Christian Peukert, Stefan Bechtold, Michail Batikas, Tobias Kretschmer
title: Regulatory Spillovers and Data Governance: Evidence from the GDPR
countries: Global website sample subject to EU regulatory spillover
period: 12 months before and 6 months after GDPR's May 2018 effectiv…
data: Panel of 110,000+ websites and their third-party HTTP requests (web technology vendors), tracked for 12 months pre- and 6 months post-GDPR
findings: Websites substantially reduced the number of third-party web-technology vendors they use after GDPR, and this reduction extended even to websites not legally bound by the GDPR, evidence of a global regulatory spillover. Market concentration in web-technology services increased after GDPR: the largest vendor (Google) lost relatively less business than smaller vendors and significantly gained share in key markets such as advertising and analytics. Effects were largest among less popular websites and for vendors collecting personal data.
magnitude: GDPR reduced websites' use of third-party vendors and increased market concentration, with Google gaining share in ad-tech/analytics even on non-EU-regulated sites

design: Purpose-built firm technology-adoption survey (FAT) covering 13,118 establishments
title: Bridging the technological divide: technology adoption by firms in developing countries
countries: Bangladesh, Brazil, Burkina Faso, Ghana, India, Kenya, Korea, Malawi, Poland, Senegal, Vietnam
data: Firm-level Adoption of Technology survey, 13,118 establishments representing about 1.3 million firms
findings: The best available measurement of what technologies firms in developing countries actually use, as opposed to what they report owning. Across 44 subnational regions in 10 countries the correlation between average technology sophistication and labour productivity is 0.87. Among the Industry 4.0 technologies — cloud computing, robots, big data, AI — cloud is the only one with meaningful firm adoption, and even that is sharply skewed towards larger firms. The authors are explicit that causal interpretations cannot be drawn from these correlations.
magnitude: 0.87 correlation between regional technology sophistication and labour productivity across 44 regions

design: Staggered rollout
findings: Evaluate the impact of introducing biometric verification into Pakistan’s Benazir Income Support Program (BISP), a national cash transfer initiative targeting over 7 million low-income women. Using a quasi-experimental design based on the staggered rollout of the Biometric Verification System (BVS) between 2017 and 2019, the study provides causal evidence on how linking fingerprint authentication to the national ID system affects outcomes. The reform required women to collect benefits in person and verify their identity biometrically at retail agents equipped with biometric point-of-sale devices. Results show that BVS increased the likelihood of women collecting cash themselves by 46 percentage points and improved their financial agency. It also raised the probability of making women decisive regarding the usage of finances by 9 percentage points among those who previously relied on intermediaries. The reform did not significantly change the net amount of cash received, but enhanced transparency and accountability in the transfer process.

design: Difference-in-differences within a local-projection framework, comparing firms in more and less digitalised industries around recessions
title: Digitalization and resilience
data: Balance-sheet data on 24,000 firms in 75 countries, combined with several industry digitalisation measures (ICT shares, robot use, online sales, intangibles, LinkedIn digital-skill listings)
findings: One of the few credible estimates of digital technology as insurance rather than as a growth input. Firms in industries one standard deviation more digitalised than average experienced roughly 2 percent smaller sales losses four years after a typical recession, and about 4 percent smaller sales declines one year into the COVID-19 recession specifically. The result is robust across five distinct measures of industry digitalisation, which matters because each measure individually is open to a different objection.
magnitude: ~4% smaller sales decline during COVID-19 for firms one standard deviation more digitalised

design: Establishment-level vacancy panel with fixed effects
authors: Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, Jonathon Hazell, Pascual Restrepo
title: AI and Jobs: Evidence from Online Vacancies
venue: Journal of Labor Economics (NBER Working Paper 28257)
data: Near-universe of online US job vacancy postings and detailed skill requirements from Burning Glass Technologies, 2010-2018
findings: AI-related vacancies grew rapidly from 2010-2018, concentrated in establishments whose workers perform tasks aligned with current AI capabilities. Establishments adopting AI simultaneously reduced hiring in non-AI positions and changed skill requirements in remaining postings, but these substitution effects were not yet large enough to be detectable in aggregate employment or wage growth across more AI-exposed occupations and industries.
magnitude: Rapid AI-vacancy growth 2010-18 at the establishment level, but no detectable aggregate employment/wage effect yet

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Provided Wikipedia access to randomly-selected students in Malawian boarding secondary schools. Students used the online resource broadly and intensively, and found it trustworthy, including for information about news and safe sex. It finds a 0.10σ impact on English exam scores, and a higher impact among low achievers (0.20σ). Students used Wikipedia to study Biology, and exam scores increased for low achievers (0.14σ). The results show that by restricting internet access to a source of engaging and accessible reading material, it is possible to encourage independent reading and affect educational outcomes.

design: Cross-sectional association
findings: Examines the relationship between AI exposure and employment growth across 23 OECD countries from 2012 to 2019. The study uses the AI occupational impact measure, which assesses the reliance of occupations on abilities where AI has made significant progress, and links this to employment data from labor force surveys. The main findings indicate no clear relationship between AI exposure and overall employment growth; however, in occupations with high computer use, AI exposure is positively associated with employment growth. Additionally, there is suggestive evidence that greater AI exposure correlates with reduced average hours worked in occupations with low computer use, potentially due to increased productivity and shifts toward higher-value tasks for workers with strong digital skills. These findings suggest that AI's impact on employment is contingent upon the digital readiness of occupations.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Show evidence that individual firms in Africa are 20 and 12 percentage points more likely to undertake process and product innovation, respectively, with access to fast internet.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Indonesia has been proactive in enhancing the remittance process for its substantial migrant worker population. Traditional remittance channels often posed risks, including high fees and potential loss of funds. To address these challenges, initiatives like Project Greenback 2.0 were introduced to promote transparent, efficient, and inclusive remittance services. This project emphasized financial education and the adoption of digital payment systems, enabling migrant workers to send money home securely and affordably. The improved remittance systems have empowered workers by providing safer financial transactions and have contributed to the economic stability of their families.

design: Difference-in-differences, Staggered rollout
findings: Used a staggered Difference-in-Differences approach, focusing on labor demand for cloud-related skills to evaluate firm productivity. The study, covering the period from 2010 to 2019, found that cloud adoption is associated with a 6.9% increase in long-term sales. A 1% increase in cloud-related labor demand leads to a 0.005% rise in firm productivity. Cloud adopters experienced a 2.24% higher productivity compared to non-adopters, translating to approximately $38.66 million in additional sales.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: SANAD Portal for Digital Government Services highlights the country’s efforts to modernize public service delivery and rebuild citizen trust through a unified, citizen-centric digital platform. Launched by the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE), SANAD integrates digital ID, biometric authentication, and over 500 transactional services, with a goal of digitizing all 2,400 government services by 2025. To date, around 810,000 digital IDs have been issued, with future expansion planned for non-citizens, including refugees. The initiative includes in-person government service centers to ensure accessibility for digitally excluded groups, alongside investments in data governance, privacy, and interoperability standards.

design: Natural experiment / administrative panel around AI dispatch-recommendation tool rollout
authors: Kyogo Kanazawa, Daiji Kawaguchi, Hitoshi Shigeoka, Yasutora Watanabe
title: AI, Skill, and Productivity: The Case of Taxi Drivers
data: Administrative trip-level data from a Japanese taxi fleet using an AI system recommending cruising routes based on predicted demand
findings: The AI navigation/dispatch tool raised overall driver productivity mainly by cutting cruising (search) time, with gains concentrated among low-skilled drivers. The productivity gap between high- and low-skilled drivers narrowed by 14%, illustrating AI's role in skill equalization rather than simple displacement.
magnitude: 14% narrowing of the high-skill/low-skill driver productivity gap

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Use a conceptual analysis approach, reviewing existing literature and industry developments related to corporate digital identity. They find that government-led digital identity systems and initiatives can reduce compliance costs for firms and risks associated with KYC processes for financial institutions. Such systems have the potential to improve efficiency in areas like trade finance by facilitating faster and more secure transactions and in supply chain management by integration with other digital systems. The paper suggests that corporate digital identity platforms can have significant impacts in these areas by reducing transaction costs and enabling new business models.

design: difference-in-differences exploiting the staggered college-by-college rollout of Facebook
authors: Luca Braghieri, Ro'ee Levy, Alexey Makarin
title: Social Media and Mental Health
data: Facebook's staggered introduction across US college campuses (2004-2006) matched to student mental-health survey data
findings: Facebook's arrival at a college campus caused a significant deterioration in student mental health, increasing the share of students screening positive for severe depression and anxiety disorders. The effect is larger for students more likely to be exposed to upward social comparisons, consistent with a social-comparison mechanism rather than simple time displacement from studying or socializing.
magnitude: Facebook's staggered rollout across US colleges caused a significant rise in severe depression and anxiety among students

design: Difference-in-differences (staggered "Broadband China" pilot-city policy rollout, 3 batches 2014-2016)
title: How does broadband infrastructure promote entrepreneurship in China: Evidence from a quasi-natural experiment
data: City-level panel data across China matched to staggered designation as a "Broadband China" demonstration pilot city (three policy batches: 2014, 2015, 2016)
findings: Cities designated as Broadband China pilots see a significant increase in new-firm registrations/entrepreneurial activity relative to non-pilot cities after designation, in a staggered difference-in-differences design around the three policy batches. The effect operates partly through lower information/communication costs and improved firm access to finance and markets.
magnitude: Broadband China pilot-city designation significantly raises new-firm entry/entrepreneurship rates relative to non-pilot cities

design: Descriptive analysis
region: Global – government-to-person payments, DPI as an approach
findings: Examined the role of digital technologies in delivering social assistance during the COVID-19 pandemic across 85 countries. The findings reveal that countries leveraging pre-pandemic investments in digital public infrastructure managed to reach an average of 51% of their population with social assistance programs, compared to only 16% in countries without such systems. Additionally, 80% of these countries utilized digital payments for aid distribution, resulting in a substantial increase in financial inclusion, with 62 countries using account-based transfers.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Examined the environmental impact of broadband infrastructure in Chile using a comparative analysis of 4G and 5G networks with both fixed and wireless backhaul options. The results indicate that 5G with a fixed fiber backhaul is the most energy-efficient strategy, emitting fewer greenhouse gases compared to other configurations. Specifically, 5G with fiber backhaul results in 32% lower nitrogen oxide emissions when increasing per-user capacity from 5 to 20 Mbps, whereas 4G with wireless backhaul results in a 151% increase. Switching off-grid diesel generators to renewable sources can reduce CO2 emissions by up to 19%.

design: Experimental/staggered-adoption variation in mandatory e-filing for firm tax returns
title: Technology, Taxation, and Corruption: Evidence from the Introduction of Electronic Tax Filing
data: Tax administration records on firm filing behavior, tax payments, and bribe payments around the 2012 e-filing rollout
findings: Use experimental variation to examine the impact of electronic tax filing (to replace in-person submission to tax officials) using data from Tajikistan firms. E-filing reduces the time firms spend on taxes by 40 percent. Further, among firms previously more likely to evade, e-filing doubles taxes paid. Conversely, evidence suggests that e-filing reduces tax payments among firms previously less likely to evade. These firms also pay fewer bribes, as e-filing reduces extortion opportunities. These patterns are consistent with differential treatment of firms by tax officials prior to e-filing.
magnitude: E-filing cut compliance time 40% and doubled tax paid by high-evasion firms

design: Structural equilibrium model of app entry/exit and usage estimated on Google Play Store panel, pre/post GDPR
authors: Rebecca Janßen, Reinhold Kesler, Michael E. Kummer, Joel Waldfogel
title: GDPR and the Lost Generation of Innovative Apps
countries: Global app market with EU regulatory treatment
data: Panel of 4.1 million apps on the Google Play Store, 2016-2019, tracking entry, exit, and usage
findings: Rebecca Janßen et al. 2022 use data on 4.1 million apps at the Google Play Store from 2016 to 2019 and document that GDPR induced the exit of about a third of available apps; and in the quarters following implementation, entry of new apps fell by half. The paper estimates a structural model of demand and entry in the app market. Comparing long-run equilibria with and without GDPR, the paper finds that GDPR reduces consumer surplus and aggregate app usage by about a third. Whatever the privacy benefits of GDPR, they come at substantial costs in foregone innovation.
magnitude: GDPR is associated with a one-third exit rate among existing apps, a roughly 50% drop in new app entry, and a one-third fall in consumer surplus and usage

design: Difference-in-differences around Apple's 2021 App Tracking Transparency (ATT) rollout
title: The Impact of Apple's App Tracking Transparency on App Monetization
data: App-level monetization and ranking data for iOS apps before and after Apple's App Tracking Transparency framework required opt-in consent for cross-app tracking
findings: Apple's ATT policy, which requires opt-in consent before apps can track users across other companies' apps and websites, reduced app monetization reliant on targeted advertising, with effects concentrated among smaller developers and ad-supported apps that depended heavily on cross-app tracking data, paralleling GDPR-style findings that privacy interventions raise compliance/adaptation costs disproportionately for smaller firms even when imposed by a platform rather than a government.
magnitude: Apple's App Tracking Transparency opt-in requirement reduced monetization for ad-supported apps, hitting smaller developers hardest

design: Large-scale field experiment with regionally clustered randomization of treatment intensity
authors: Steffen Altmann, Anita Marie Glenny, Robert Mahlstedt, Alexander Sebald
title: The Direct and Indirect Effects of Online Job Search Advice
data: Large sample of unemployed job seekers randomized into an online dashboard providing vacancy information and occupation recommendations, with region-level variation in treatment saturation
findings: In regions with low treatment intensity (under 50% of job seekers treated), the online job-search advice tool raised earnings and hours worked by 8.5-9.5% in the following year. At higher treatment saturation, gains were eroded by substantial negative spillovers on other treated job seekers, as increased competition for similar vacancies offset much of the aggregate benefit.
magnitude: Online job-search advice raised earnings 8.5-9.5% at low treatment saturation, but congestion erased gains at high saturation

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Studies individuals’ use of internet, specifically among the poor. They collaborate with a Kenyan telecom to provide free phone data to poor subscribers who had not used data in the previous year but owned a data-capable phone. The study randomly selected recipients and found that, while data usage moderately increased, there were no significant changes in economic outcomes like employment or consumption. These findings suggest that subsidizing and encouraging use of existing mobile internet access among priced-out (or reluctant) individuals is unlikely to be effective in settings like Kenya.

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Analyzed the effect of internet adoption on female labor market outcomes using a difference-in-differences approach between 2010 and 2016. 1% increase in internet access resulted in a 0.7% increase in female labor force participation, particularly among unmarried women. Also, internet adoption led to declines in marriage and fertility rates among these women (no significant impact on male labor market outcomes).

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Wandaogo, 2022 analyze the effect of digitalization on government effectiveness in developing and developed countries. They use a panel methodology with data from 138 countries between 2006 and 2016. The results suggest that a government’s use of information and communication technologies (ICT) improves its effectiveness in both developing and developed countries. However, this effect is stronger in developed than in developing countries. The effect of aggregate ICT use by individuals, businesses, and government on overall government effectiveness is greater than that of individual use by each individually. The results are robust after several tests (reverse causality, dynamic effect, sensitivity analysis, heterogeneities, and alternative measurements). These results highlight the fact that governments could fully benefit from digitalization by adopting policies that promote access to and use of ICT at all levels of the economy, that is, the government itself, businesses, and individuals.

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Broadband Demonstration City program in China in 2014. Variations in broadband development across time and between demonstration and ordinary cities. Difference-in-difference estimates show that the deployment of high-quality broadband promoted regional employment in the skilled service sector in China. Compared to ordinary cities, total employment in the broadband demonstration city increased by 3 percent, the positive impact of broadband on employment is larger in innovation-related industries, including education (2.7 percent), ICT (19.7 percent), and scientific research sectors (9.2 percent). The effect was larger in cities with a greater number of educated residents and cities in the west of China. (Wang, Xu, Huang, and Yang 2022)

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Investigated the impact of the "Broadband China" pilot policy (i.e. Internet development) on urban eco-efficiency using a multi-period and spatial difference-in-difference method. The study, which analyzed data from 285 prefecture-level cities between 2005 and 2019, found that the policy significantly improved eco-efficiency, with pilot cities exhibiting a 16.8% higher eco-efficiency than non-pilot cities. The policy's effects were more pronounced in central, eastern, and northeastern regions compared to the western region. The policy's positive effects extend beyond local cities, enhancing eco-efficiency in neighboring cities due to spatial spillover effects. The improved Internet infrastructure drives technological progress and resource optimization.

design: Cross-sectional association
findings: Analyzed the digital business landscape from 1970 to 2020 across 190 countries. Digital business density showed a strong positive correlation with market size and population, with high-performing countries like Estonia and Kenya exceeding expectations. Approximately 60% of digital firms operate in more than one product market, indicating scope economies. Platform-based and data-driven business models were prevalent, particularly in e-Commerce and FinTech. US and Chinese investors dominated global digital investments, focusing mainly on domestic markets. Digital firms in developed countries displayed greater market maturity with higher exit rates and larger exit sizes compared to those in developing countries.

design: Cross-sectional association
findings: Use a sample of 3,300 firms across seven Sub-Saharan African countries to study the use of digital technologies, their association with performance outcomes. The analysis finds that productive use of digital technologies is low: less than 7 percent of firms use a smartphone, less than 6 percent use a computer, and roughly 20 percent still do not use a mobile phone. Internet-enabled computers and smartphones usage is associated with higher job levels.

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Assessed the impact of work-from-home (WFH) feasibility on firm performance using a difference-in-differences approach. The study, covering the period from 2010 to 2019, found that firms with high pre-pandemic WFH feasibility experienced a 15% increase in net income and a 4% rise in sales during the pandemic compared to firms with lower WFH feasibility. These firms also exhibited better stock market performance, with a 4.3% higher abnormal return and lower return volatility. Notably, firms in non-essential industries with high WFH feasibility saw more significant benefits than those in essential industries.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Conduct a case study of 8 e-government projects in India for an impact assessment. In the CARD project, the average number of trips to government offices reduced from 2.7 to 1.4, with transactions and revenues growing by 50% from 2002-03, while costs increased by only 6%. The Bhoomi project saw waiting times decrease from 2.5 hours to 30 minutes on average, and bribery dropped from 30% to less than 1%. Additionally, the eProcurement platform realized cost savings of 20% in 2003-04 and 12% in 2004-05 due to increased competition among suppliers.

design: systematic review of ICT carbon-footprint estimates and system boundaries
authors: Charlotte Freitag, Mike Berners-Lee, Kelly Widdicks, Bran Knowles, Gordon Blair, Adrian Friday
title: The climate impact of ICT: A review of estimates, trends and regulations
